categories.texte:
✨ EXHIBIT A: QURANIC FOUNDATION
Surah At-Tawbah, v.34: 'Those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend it in the way of Allah - give them tidings of a painful punishment.'

✨ EXHIBIT B: AUTHENTIC HADITH
Reported by Amr ibn Shu'ayb (Abu Dawud No. 1563, Authenticated), the Prophet ﷺ saw a woman with her daughter wearing two heavy gold bracelets. He said: 'Do you pay Zakat on this?' She said: 'No.' He said: 'Would it please you that Allah clothe you with two bracelets of fire on the Day of Resurrection?'

✨ EXHIBIT C: FIQH OF THE FOUR SCHOOLS (SUNNI)
• Hanafi School: Strict taxation at 2.5% of all gold owned, personal use as jewelry not changing its taxable nature.
• Maliki, Shafi'i, Hanbali Schools: Exemption of a woman's lawful personal jewelry. Only investment or savings gold is subject to the tax.

quiz.question: According to the Hanafi school, is gold jewelry worn by a woman subject to Zakat?
quiz.explication: The Hanafi school taxes 2.5% of all gold owned: wearing it as jewelry does not change its taxable nature.

quiz.question: Which schools exempt a woman's lawful personal jewelry from Zakat?
quiz.explication: Only investment or savings gold is taxed among the Maliki, Shafi'i, and Hanbali schools.

quiz.question: In the hadith reported by Abu Dawud, what was the woman questioned by the Prophet ﷺ wearing?
quiz.explication: The Prophet ﷺ asked her whether she paid Zakat on it, before the warning about the bracelets of fire.

categories.texte:
✨ EXHIBIT A: QURANIC FOUNDATION
Surah Al-An'am, v.141: 'And render its due [zakat] on the day of its harvest.'

✨ EXHIBIT B: AUTHENTIC HADITH
Reported by Jabir (Muslim No. 981), the Prophet ﷺ said: 'For what is watered by the sky or by springs, one-tenth (10%) is due. For what is watered artificially, one-twentieth (5%) is due.' The threshold (Nisab) is set at 5 Wasaqs (approximately 653 kg).

✨ EXHIBIT C: FIQH OF THE FOUR SCHOOLS (SUNNI)
Unanimous consensus on the irrigation rates. Regarding livestock, the official charter of Abu Bakr (Al-Bukhari No. 1454) sets the threshold for sheep: 40 to 120 sheep = 1 sheep due. Below 40 head, no Zakat is due.

quiz.question: What Zakat rate applies to a naturally irrigated harvest (rain, springs)?
quiz.explication: The full tithe (10%) is due for natural irrigation; the half tithe (5%) for artificial irrigation.

quiz.question: What is the minimum number of sheep one must own before Zakat on livestock becomes due?
quiz.explication: Below 40 head, no Zakat is due; from 40 to 120, only one sheep is due.

quiz.question: The Nisab threshold for harvests roughly corresponds to what weight?
quiz.explication: The agricultural Nisab is set at 5 Wasaqs, or approximately 653 kg.

categories.texte:
✨ EXHIBIT A: QURANIC FOUNDATION
Surah At-Tawbah, v.103: 'Take, [O Muhammad], from their wealth a charity (Sadaqah) by which you purify them and cause them increase.'

✨ EXHIBIT B: AUTHENTIC HADITH
Reported by Ibn 'Umar (Al-Bukhari No. 1454), the Prophet ﷺ set the gold threshold at a precise weight before any levy: below it, no Zakat is due, regardless of how long it has been held. This threshold principle (Nisab) protects the modest believer from any unwarranted levy.

✨ EXHIBIT C: FIQH OF THE FOUR SCHOOLS (SUNNI)
The four schools agree on the reference thresholds: 85 grams of pure gold, or 595 grams of pure silver. The divergence concerns which of the two to use when their market values differ:
• Historical majority position: use the gold threshold, more stable over time.
• Position widely held among contemporaries: use whichever threshold is lower (converted at the current rate), which triggers Zakat sooner and better protects needy beneficiaries (Masakin). This cautious position is the one most modern Zakat calculators apply by default.

quiz.question: At how many grams of pure gold is the Nisab threshold traditionally set?
quiz.explication: The four schools agree on 85 g of pure gold (or 595 g of pure silver) as the reference threshold.

quiz.question: What happens if a believer's net wealth is below the Nisab?
choix: They must still pay 2.5% as a precaution
No Zakat is due, regardless of how long it has been held
They must pay half the normal rate
quiz.explication: The Nisab is a strict threshold: below it, there is simply no Zakat obligation.

quiz.question: Why do most contemporary calculators use whichever threshold is lower between gold and silver?
choix: To trigger Zakat sooner and better protect the needy
Because it is the only permitted position
quiz.explication: This is a position of doctrinal caution, not a single fixed rule: it maximizes the share reserved for beneficiaries.

categories.texte:
✨ EXHIBIT A: QURANIC FOUNDATION
Surah An-Nisa, v.11: The distribution of shares occurs only after applying the overriding clause: '...after any bequest which was made or debt.'

✨ EXHIBIT B: AUTHENTIC HADITH
Reported by Salamah ibn al-Akwa' (Al-Bukhari No. 2289), a deceased man was brought to the Prophet ﷺ for him to pray over. He asked: 'Did he leave any debt?' They said: 'Yes, three dinars.' He said: 'Pray over your companion (I will not pray over him)' until a companion guaranteed the debt.

✨ EXHIBIT C: FIQH OF THE FOUR SCHOOLS (SUNNI)
• Passive Debts: Absolute priority over inheritance and the Wasiyya. Among the Maliki and Hanbali schools, they also reduce the taxable base for financial Zakat.
• Active Debts (Receivables): If recoverable (solvent debtor), the Hanafi school requires Zakat every year, while the Maliki school requires payment only once, at the time of recovery.

quiz.question: According to the hadith of Salamah ibn al-Akwa', how many dinars did the deceased owe?
quiz.explication: The Prophet ﷺ refused to pray over him until a companion guaranteed these 3 dinars.

quiz.question: What must imperatively be settled before the inheritance distribution?
quiz.explication: Surah An-Nisa v.11: the distribution occurs only after execution of the will and payment of debts.

quiz.question: For a recoverable receivable, which school requires Zakat every year?
quiz.explication: The Maliki school requires a single payment at the time of recovery, unlike the Hanafi school.

categories.texte:
✨ EXHIBIT A: QURANIC FOUNDATION
Surah An-Nisa, v.11: 'Allah instructs you concerning your children: for the male, what is equal to the share of two females.'

✨ EXHIBIT B: AUTHENTIC HADITH
Reported by Ibn Abbas (Al-Bukhari No. 6732, Muslim No. 1615), the Prophet ﷺ said: 'Give the fixed shares (Fara'idh) to those entitled to them. What remains after that goes to the closest male relative of the deceased.'

✨ EXHIBIT C: FIQH OF THE FOUR SCHOOLS (SUNNI)
Absolute consensus on the double-ratio distribution. This rule is tied to the financial maintenance obligation (Nafaqah) that falls exclusively on the man. The woman retains her entire share for her private use, with no obligation to spend on the household. Potential beneficiaries include descendants, ascendants, collaterals (brothers, sisters, full and paternal uncles, nephews, cousins), and the surviving spouse.

quiz.question: According to the Quran (An-Nisa v.11), what is the son's share compared to the daughter's?
quiz.explication: "For the male, what is equal to the share of two females" — the base ratio is 2 to 1.

quiz.question: According to the hadith reported by Ibn Abbas, who receives the remainder after the fixed shares?
choix: The closest male relative of the deceased
It is redistributed equally among all
quiz.explication: "What remains after that goes to the closest male relative of the deceased" — this is the principle of Asabah.

quiz.question: What financial obligation justifies the 2-to-1 ratio in favor of men?
quiz.explication: The man bears the household's financial burden; the woman keeps her share with no obligation to spend it.

categories.titre: 🧮 MODULE: Al-Aoul and Ar-Radd — When the Shares Don't Add Up to 1
categories.texte:
✨ EXHIBIT A: THE STARTING TENSION (QURAN)
Surah An-Nisa, v.11-12 sets precise shares (1/2, 1/3, 1/6, 1/4, 1/8...) for several categories of heirs at once. Depending on the exact family composition, the sum of these fractions can, in some cases, exceed one whole — or, conversely, fall short of it if there is no residuary heir (Asabah) to absorb the remainder.

✨ EXHIBIT B: THE JURISPRUDENTIAL RESPONSE (AL-AOUL)
As reported in the major treatises of inheritance Fiqh, the first case of oversaturation is said to have been submitted to Caliph 'Umar ibn Al-Khattab: a husband (1/2) and two full sisters (2/3) together claim 7/6 of the same estate — more than the total available. On the suggestion of the companion Zayd ibn Thabit, the solution adopted was to proportionally expand the common denominator (here from 6 to 7) rather than favor one heir over another: each fixed share shrinks slightly, but none is eliminated.

✨ EXHIBIT C: FIQH OF THE FOUR SCHOOLS (SUNNI)
• Al-Aoul (oversaturation): consensus of the four schools on the principle — when the sum of shares exceeds 1, the denominator is expanded (6→7, 8, 9 or 10; 12→13, 15, 17; 24→27) to distribute the shortfall proportionally among all fixed-share heirs.
• Ar-Radd (return/reversion): if the sum of shares is less than 1 and there is no residuary heir (Asabah), should the surplus go back to the fixed-share heirs, or to the public treasury (Bayt Al-Mal)? The Hanafi and Hanbali schools (and later Shafi'i jurisprudence) redistribute the surplus proportionally among the blood-related heirs, excluding the husband or wife. The classical Maliki school rejects this mechanism and would direct the surplus to the public treasury.

quiz.question: What does the Al-Aoul mechanism do when the sum of fixed shares exceeds 1?
choix: It cancels the share of the last heir added
It expands the common denominator to proportionally reduce each share
It transfers the excess to the public treasury
quiz.explication: No heir is excluded: the denominator expands (for example from 6 to 7) and each share shrinks accordingly.

quiz.question: Which companion is associated with the first resolution of the oversaturation case under Caliph 'Umar?
quiz.explication: It was Zayd ibn Thabit who is said to have suggested expanding the denominator, a solution that remains the classical reference.

quiz.question: Which school classically rejects the Ar-Radd mechanism (returning the surplus to the heirs)?
quiz.explication: The classical Maliki school instead directs any undistributed surplus to the public treasury (Bayt Al-Mal).

categories.texte:
✨ EXHIBIT A: QURANIC FOUNDATION
Surah An-Nisa, v.12: 'And if a man or woman leaves neither ascendants nor descendants (Kalalah) but has a brother or a sister (uterine), then for each one of them is a sixth. But if they are more than two, they share a third.'

✨ EXHIBIT B: AUTHENTIC HADITH
Asked about the exact meaning of Kalalah, Caliph Abu Bakr As-Siddiq (validated by the consensus of the companions) said: 'Kalalah is one who has neither descendant (child) nor direct male ascendant (father/grandfather).'

✨ EXHIBIT C: FIQH OF THE FOUR SCHOOLS (SUNNI)
In the Kalalah case, maternal siblings (uterine, through the mother) inherit in strictly equal shares between men and women (a unique exception to the double ratio). Full siblings, on the other hand, receive the remainder as residuary heirs (Asabah).

quiz.question: How did Caliph Abu Bakr define Kalalah?
choix: One who has neither descendant nor direct male ascendant
One who is orphaned of their father
quiz.explication: Neither child, nor father, nor grandfather — this is the definition validated by the consensus of the companions.

quiz.question: In the Kalalah case, how is the inheritance shared between uterine brothers and sisters?
choix: Equal share between men and women
quiz.explication: This is the sole exception to the usual 2-to-1 ratio.

quiz.question: If more than two uterine brothers/sisters are involved, what fraction do they share?
quiz.explication: At two or fewer, one sixth each; beyond that, they share the third.

categories.titre: 🏛️ MODULE: A Historical Ruling — The Himariyya
categories.texte:
✨ EXHIBIT A: THE STARTING CASE (QURAN)
Surah An-Nisa, v.12 grants uterine brothers and sisters (through the mother) a fixed share of 1/3 when there are several of them. A rare case puts this rule under tension: a husband, a mother, and several uterine siblings combined already exhaust the entire estate (1/2 + 1/6 + 1/3 = 1), theoretically leaving nothing for the full brother (same father AND mother), who would normally inherit as a residuary heir (Asabah).

✨ EXHIBIT B: THE RULING ATTRIBUTED TO 'UMAR IBN AL-KHATTAB
This case is reported in the great classical treatises of Fara'id. The first time, Caliph 'Umar is said to have ruled according to the strict letter of the text: the full brother, being a residuary heir with nothing left to collect, received nothing. The following year, the same case arose again; the full brother is reported to have appealed to the caliph, in essence: he and the uterine siblings share the same mother — why exclude him entirely when the only thing distinguishing them is a father left out of the calculation? Persuaded by this argument of fairness, 'Umar is said to have revised his position and admitted the full brother to share the third reserved for the uterine siblings, in equal parts.
⚠️ Note of caution: as with many reports from the era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs, the exact details of the wording vary depending on the source; it is the principle retained by later jurisprudence that stands as the reference, more than the exact quotation.

✨ EXHIBIT C: FIQH OF THE FOUR SCHOOLS (SUNNI)
• Maliki and Shafi'i schools: adopt 'Umar's second position. The full brother(s) join(s) the uterine siblings in their Quranic third, shared in strictly equal parts among all (an exception, as with the uterine siblings themselves, to the usual double ratio for men).
• Hanafi and Hanbali schools: retain the original literal rule. Since the full brother's residual share is nil, he receives nothing in this specific case — HAYAATI displays this explicitly as 0 rather than omitting him from the table, for full transparency of the calculation.

quiz.question: In the Himariyya case, which heirs exhaust the estate before the full brother?
choix: The husband, the mother, and the uterine brothers/sisters
The father and the paternal uncles
quiz.explication: Husband (1/2) + Mother (1/6) + Uterine siblings (1/3) = exactly 1: theoretically nothing is left for the residuary heir.

quiz.question: According to the second position attributed to 'Umar ibn Al-Khattab, what happens to the full brother in this case?
choix: He is permanently excluded from the inheritance
He shares the uterine siblings' third in equal parts
He receives the entire third, alone
quiz.explication: The argument of the shared maternal bond led to including him in the third reserved for the uterine siblings, on equal footing with them.

quiz.question: Which schools retain the original literal rule (full brother excluded) in this specific case?
quiz.explication: The Maliki and Shafi'i schools adopted 'Umar's second position; the Hanafi and Hanbali schools retain the first.

categories.titre: 📝 MODULE: The Will and the One-Third Ceiling
categories.texte:
✨ EXHIBIT A: QURANIC FOUNDATION
Surah Al-Baqarah, v.180: 'It is prescribed for you, when death approaches one of you, if he leaves wealth, that he make a bequest for parents and near relatives...'

✨ EXHIBIT B: AUTHENTIC HADITH
Reported by Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas (Al-Bukhari No. 2744, Muslim No. 1628), the Prophet ﷺ said to him while he was ill and wanted to give all his wealth in charity: 'Give a third. And a third is already a great deal. It is better that you leave your heirs wealthy than leave them poor, holding out their hands to people.'

✨ EXHIBIT C: FIQH OF THE FOUR SCHOOLS (SUNNI)
Unanimous consensus: The Wasiyya is strictly forbidden in favor of a legal heir (except with the unanimous agreement of the other heirs after death), and it is capped at a maximum of one third (1/3) of the net estate after settlement of debts. The application automatically blocks any excess.

quiz.question: What is the maximum limit of the Wasiyya (will) relative to the net estate?
quiz.explication: Unanimous consensus of the four schools: a maximum of one third, after settlement of debts.

quiz.question: What did the Prophet ﷺ answer Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, who wanted to give everything in charity?
choix: "Give a third, and a third is already a great deal"
quiz.explication: He added: it is better to leave one's heirs wealthy than poor and holding out their hands.

quiz.question: Can a legal heir who already has a fixed share also receive a bequest by will?
choix: No, except with the unanimous agreement of the other heirs
quiz.explication: A Wasiyya in favor of a legal heir is forbidden except when unanimously approved by the other heirs after death.

categories.texte:
✨ EXHIBIT A: QURANIC FOUNDATION
Surah Al-Hashr, v.18: 'O you who have believed, fear Allah. And let every soul look to what it has put forth for tomorrow.'

✨ EXHIBIT B: AUTHENTIC HADITH
• On the White Days (At-Tirmidhi No. 761, Authentic): The Prophet ﷺ said: 'If you fast three days of the month, fast the 13th, 14th, and 15th.' Fasting these days is equivalent to fasting for a lifetime.
• On supererogatory prayers (Muslim No. 728): The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Whoever prays twelve supererogatory Rak'ahs each day, Allah will build for him a house in Paradise.'

✨ EXHIBIT C: FIQH OF THE FOUR SCHOOLS (SUNNI)
Consensus on the highly meritorious nature (Sunnah Mu'akkadah) of the attached prayers (Rawatib) and the fasting of the White Days, essential tools for the daily purification of the soul.

quiz.question: Which days of the month correspond to the "White Days" recommended for fasting?
quiz.explication: Reported by At-Tirmidhi: fasting these three days is equivalent to fasting for a lifetime.

quiz.question: How many daily supererogatory Rak'ahs are associated with the promise of a house in Paradise?
quiz.explication: Reported by Muslim: twelve Rak'ahs of Rawatib each day.

quiz.question: Which verse of Surah Al-Hashr urges every soul to look at what it has prepared for tomorrow?
quiz.explication: "And let every soul look to what it has put forth for tomorrow."

temps.note_pedagogique: The future does not change the conjugation: it simply adds a prefix before the present tense. سَـ (sa-) for a near or general future — the form shown here. سَوْفَ (sawfa), written separately, for a more distant or emphasized future: سَوْفَ يَذْهَبُ (sawfa yadhhabu) has the same meaning as سَيَذْهَبُ, with an added nuance of distance or emphasis.

conjugaisons.sens: the two of them (m.) will go
the two of them (f.) will go
the two of you will go
the two of you will go

temps.note_pedagogique: The imperative only exists in the 2nd person ('you') — one can only directly command the person being addressed. To say 'let's go' or 'let him go', Arabic uses a different construction (لِـ + jussive), which we'll see later. Here, only 5 forms, not 14: the 2nd person dual has no masc./fem. distinction. Another key point: depending on the verb, the imperative's hamza is not always pronounced the same way — see the 3 rules below before the cards.

regles_type_verbe.regle: When the vowel on the second-to-last letter of the present tense is a damma (ُ), the imperative's hamza also takes a damma.
When this vowel is a fatha or a kasra, the imperative's hamza takes a kasra — this is the case for our model verb ذهب.

For hollow verbs (whose 2nd root letter is و or ي, like نَامَ), this letter disappears in the جزم mode: what remains after removing the prefix is already pronounceable on its own, with no supporting vowel needed.

temps.note_temporelle: The imperative and the prohibitive have no tense of their own, neither past nor future: by nature, a command always refers to an action that has not yet happened — the future is already built into the very meaning of these two moods. To report a command in the past or future (indirect speech), Arabic switches construction: an ordinary verb (أَمَرَ / نَهَى) followed by أَنْ + a verb in the مَنْصُوب (subjunctive).

exemples_temporels.sens: he ordered him to go (command reported in the past)
he will order him to go (command reported in the future)
he forbade him to go (prohibition reported in the past)

temps.note_pedagogique: The prohibitive ('don't do') is formed with لَا + the verb in the جزم mode (jussive — the same ending as the negative future). Structure: لَا + the present tense form with the imperative ending. Unlike the Amr, the Nahy has no hamza-vowel issue at all: the present tense's تَـ prefix always stays in place, لا simply comes before it.

lecons.titre: 1. الكلمة وأقسامها - The Three Types of Words
lecons.explication:
Every Arabic word belongs to one of three categories: اسم (noun), فِعْل (verb), or حَرْف (particle). Knowing which one changes everything, because each behaves differently within a sentence.

The اسم (noun) can be preceded by the article الـ, take tanwin (ـٌ ـً ـٍ), and act as a subject. The فِعْل (verb) is conjugated across tenses — exactly what we handled in the previous stage with ذَهَبَ / يَذْهَبُ / سَيَذْهَبُ. The حَرْف (particle) only takes on meaning when attached to a noun or verb: on its own, it means nothing.

exemples.sens: a book (اسم — accepts الـ and tanwin)
he wrote (فِعْل — conjugates)
in (حَرْف — only has meaning with a word after it)

lecons.titre: 2. الجملة الاسمية - The Nominal Sentence
lecons.explication:
The nominal sentence is built from two blocks: the مُبْتَدَأ (the subject being discussed, almost always definite) and the خَبَر (what is said about it, the new information). Both normally take the مرفوع case (nominative), recognizable by the damma ـُ or the tanwin ـٌ.

In « البيتُ جميلٌ » (the house is beautiful): البيتُ is the مبتدأ — made definite by الـ, so we already know what is being talked about. جميلٌ is the خبر — indefinite, marked with tanwin, it is the new information being provided.

exemples.sens: the house is beautiful (مبتدأ + خبر)
the book is useful

lecons.titre: 3. المذكر والمؤنث - Masculine and Feminine
lecons.explication:
Most feminine nouns and adjectives are recognized by the final ة (tā' marbūta), pronounced as a light 'a' in pause. Adding this letter to a masculine word generally makes it feminine.

Exceptions to know: some words are feminine by nature, with no written marker at all — they behave as feminine in agreement even though nothing signals it visually.

exemples.sens: a male student / a female student
mother (feminine without ة — exception to memorize)

lecons.titre: 4. المفرد والمثنى والجمع - Singular, Dual, Plural
lecons.explication:
Arabic distinguishes three numbers, not two: المفرد (singular, one), المثنى (dual, exactly two, with its own ending ـَانِ), and الجمع (plural, three or more).

The plural is formed in two ways: جمع سالم ('sound plural', regular, a predictable ending is added), or جمع تكسير ('broken plural', the word's internal form changes, to be learned case by case — this is the most common case for everyday nouns).

exemples.sens: a book (مفرد — singular)
two books (مثنى — dual, ending ـَانِ)
books (جمع تكسير — broken plural, the form changes entirely)

lecons.titre: 5. المعرفة والنكرة - Definite and Indefinite
lecons.explication:
النكرة (indefinite) refers to an unspecified thing, generally marked by tanwin: « رَجُلٌ » means 'a man', any man at all.

المعرفة (definite) takes several forms: a noun preceded by الـ (« الرَّجُلُ », that specific man), proper nouns (already definite by nature, even with tanwin), pronouns (هو، أنتَ، أنا...), and demonstratives (هذا، هذه...) — all of them refer to something specific without needing الـ.

exemples.sens: a man (نكرة — indefinite)
the man, this man (معرفة — definite via الـ)
this one (معرفة — definite by nature)

lecons.titre: 1. الاسم الجامد - The Base Noun
lecons.explication: An الاسم الجامد is a 'base' noun, not derived from a verb: it is a simple word, with no direct morphological link to a verbal root. Most everyday concrete nouns fall into this category.

exemples.sens: a man (jamid — base word)
a stone (jamid)

lecons.titre: 2. الاسم المشتق - The Derived Noun
lecons.explication:
An الاسم المشتق is built from a verbal root: it carries the meaning of the action. The two most useful derivatives to know:

اسم الفَاعِل (agent noun): 'the one who does...'. اسم المَفْعُول (patient noun): 'that which undergoes... / that which has been done'. These two derivatives are built directly from the verb forms of the next section (الأوزان) — the bridge between the two is direct.

exemples.sens: a writer, one who writes (اسم الفاعل, from كَتَبَ)
written, that which has been written (اسم المفعول, from كَتَبَ)

lecons.titre: ٣. مقدمة - A Classification by Meaning, Not by Form
lecons.explication:
This classification differs from the جامد/مشتق pair seen just before: it does not look at how the word is built, but at the nature of what it refers to. This is exactly the logic of the traditional Arabic game « إنسان، حيوان، نبات، جماد » (sometimes extended with بلاد, a country): given a letter, you must find a word in each category.

Careful not to confuse the two: جماد here means 'that which is inanimate' (a category of meaning, coming up), whereas الاسم الجامد from the previous lesson means 'a word not derived from a verb' (a category of construction). Same root, two different ideas — keep the two meanings clearly separate.

lecons.titre: ٤. إِنْسَان (Insān) - The Human Being
lecons.explication: This category groups everything that refers to a person: proper names, professions, family roles, types of people.

exemples.sens: Ahmed (proper name of a person)
doctor (profession)
mother (family role)
man (type of person)

lecons.titre: ٥. حَيَوَان - The Animal
lecons.explication: Any living creature that moves on its own: mammals, birds, insects, fish.

exemples.sens: lion
bird (sparrow)
ant

lecons.titre: ٦. نَبَات - The Plant
lecons.explication: Everything that grows from the earth: fruits, vegetables, trees, flowers, grasses.

exemples.sens: apple
tree
flower, rose

lecons.titre: ٧. جَمَاد - The Inanimate
lecons.explication: Solid objects, manufactured or natural, without life: they do not move on their own, do not grow, do not breathe.

exemples.sens: table
pen
stone

lecons.titre: ٨. شَيْء - The Thing, the Abstract
lecons.explication: A broader category: concepts, ideas, feelings, natural phenomena — everything that does not clearly fit into the four previous categories.

exemples.sens: love
idea
rain

lecons.titre: 1. Form I (المجرد) - the simple verb — وزن فَعَلَ
lecons.explication:
The base form, with no added letter. All other forms derive from it by adding letters to the root.

صِيغَة صَغِيرَة (Sighah Saghirah) — the summary table of this verb's key forms, on the root ف-ع-ل:

exemples.sens: he wrote
الماضي — the past
المضارع — the present
المصدر — the verbal noun (varies a lot in Form I)
اسم الفاعل — the doer of the action
اسم المفعول — the receiver of the action
الأمر — direct command

lecons.titre: 2. Form II — وزن فَعَّلَ
lecons.explication:
Doubling of the 2nd root letter. Often causative or intensive: عَلِمَ (to know) → عَلَّمَ (to make known, to teach).

صِيغَة صَغِيرَة (Sighah Saghirah) — the summary table of this verb's key forms, on the root ف-ع-ل:

exemples.sens: he taught
الماضي — the past
المضارع — the present
المصدر — the verbal noun
اسم الفاعل — the doer of the action
اسم المفعول — the receiver of the action
الأمر — direct command

lecons.titre: 3. Form III — وزن فَاعَلَ
lecons.explication:
Alif after the 1st root letter. Often an action directed at someone, or a shared effort.

صِيغَة صَغِيرَة (Sighah Saghirah) — the summary table of this verb's key forms, on the root ف-ع-ل:

exemples.sens: he corresponded (in writing) with someone
الماضي — the past
المضارع — the present
المصدر — the verbal noun (two possible forms)
اسم الفاعل — the doer of the action
اسم المفعول — the receiver of the action
الأمر — direct command

lecons.titre: 4. Form IV — وزن أَفْعَلَ
lecons.explication:
Hamza as a prefix. Often causative: كَرُمَ (to be noble) → أَكْرَمَ (to honor).

صِيغَة صَغِيرَة (Sighah Saghirah) — the summary table of this verb's key forms, on the root ف-ع-ل:

exemples.sens: he honored
الماضي — the past
المضارع — the present
المصدر — the verbal noun
اسم الفاعل — the doer of the action
اسم المفعول — the receiver of the action
الأمر — direct command

lecons.titre: 5. Form V — وزن تَفَعَّلَ
lecons.explication:
Prefix تَـ + doubling. Reflexive of Form II: عَلَّمَ (to teach) → تَعَلَّمَ (to learn by oneself).

صِيغَة صَغِيرَة (Sighah Saghirah) — the summary table of this verb's key forms, on the root ف-ع-ل:

exemples.sens: he learned
الماضي — the past
المضارع — the present
المصدر — the verbal noun
اسم الفاعل — the doer of the action
اسم المفعول — the receiver of the action
الأمر — direct command

lecons.titre: 6. Form VI — وزن تَفَاعَلَ
lecons.explication:
Prefix تَـ + alif. Reciprocal of Form III: a mutual action, shared between several people.

صِيغَة صَغِيرَة (Sighah Saghirah) — the summary table of this verb's key forms, on the root ف-ع-ل:

exemples.sens: they wrote to each other
الماضي — the past
المضارع — the present
المصدر — the verbal noun
اسم الفاعل — the doer of the action
اسم المفعول — the receiver of the action
الأمر — direct command

lecons.titre: 7. Form VII — وزن اِنْفَعَلَ
lecons.explication:
Infixed نْ. Passive or autonomous reflexive: كَسَرَ (to break) → اِنْكَسَرَ (to break, to become broken).

صِيغَة صَغِيرَة (Sighah Saghirah) — the summary table of this verb's key forms, on the root ف-ع-ل:

exemples.sens: it broke
الماضي — the past
المضارع — the present
المصدر — the verbal noun
اسم الفاعل — the doer of the action
اسم المفعول — nonexistent: this form is always intransitive
الأمر — direct command

lecons.titre: 8. Form VIII — وزن اِفْتَعَلَ
lecons.explication:
Infixed تْ after the 1st root letter. Reflexive or for oneself: جَمَعَ (to gather) → اِجْتَمَعَ (to gather together).

صِيغَة صَغِيرَة (Sighah Saghirah) — the summary table of this verb's key forms, on the root ف-ع-ل:

exemples.sens: he gathered, met with others
الماضي — the past
المضارع — the present
المصدر — the verbal noun
اسم الفاعل — the doer of the action
اسم المفعول — the receiver of the action
الأمر — direct command

lecons.titre: 9. Form IX — وزن اِفْعَلَّ
lecons.explication:
Doubling of the last root letter. Reserved almost exclusively for colors and physical defects.

صِيغَة صَغِيرَة (Sighah Saghirah) — the summary table of this verb's key forms, on the root ف-ع-ل:

exemples.sens: he turned red, he blushed
الماضي — the past
المضارع — the present
المصدر — the verbal noun
اسم الفاعل — the doer of the action
اسم المفعول — nonexistent: purely intransitive form
الأمر — direct command

lecons.titre: 10. Form X — وزن اِسْتَفْعَلَ
lecons.explication:
Prefix اِسْتَـ. Often 'to seek, to ask for, to consider as': غَفَرَ (to forgive) → اِسْتَغْفَرَ (to seek/ask for forgiveness).

exemples.sens: he asked for forgiveness

lecons.titre: 1. حروف الجر - Prepositions
lecons.explication: These particles always attach to a noun, which then takes the مجرور case (genitive, marked by the kasra ـِ). Three of them (بِـ، لِـ، كَـ) are written directly attached to the following word, with no space.

exemples.sens: from, since
to, towards
on
in
with, by (attached)
for, to (attached)

lecons.titre: 2. حروف العطف - Coordinating Conjunctions
lecons.explication: They connect two words or two clauses of equal status. وَ and فَ are also written attached to the following word.

exemples.sens: and
then, so (immediate)
then (with a delay)
or

lecons.titre: 3. حروف النفي - Negation Particles
lecons.explication: Arabic chooses its negation according to the tense being targeted: it is not a single particle for everything, unlike English 'not'.

exemples.sens: not (present, general)
not (past — followed by the jussive)
never (future — followed by the subjunctive)
not (past, common usage)

lecons.titre: 1. الجملة الاسمية والفعلية - The Two Types of Sentences
lecons.explication:
Arabic distinguishes two main sentence types, based on what comes first.

The الجملة الاسمية (nominal sentence) begins with a noun: this is the one we saw with مبتدأ/خبر.

The الجملة الفعلية (verbal sentence) begins with a conjugated verb, followed by its subject. This is the normal word order in Arabic: verb first, subject after — the opposite of English.

exemples.sens: the house is beautiful (جملة اسمية — begins with a noun)
the boy left, lit. 'left the-boy' (جملة فعلية — begins with the verb)

lecons.titre: 2. الجملة الاستفهامية - The Interrogative Sentence
lecons.explication:
To ask a closed (yes/no) question, Arabic simply adds هَلْ or أَ before the sentence — the internal structure does not change.

هَلْ is used in most neutral cases. أَ (a simple hamza attached to the following word) is more literary and is also used to offer a choice (أَ ... أَمْ ... = is it... or...).

exemples.sens: are you a student?

exemples.arabe: أَأَنْتَ مِنَ الهِنْدِ أَمْ مِنْ بَاكِسْتَانَ؟
exemples.translitteration: a-anta mina al-hindi am min bākistān?
exemples.sens: are you from India or from Pakistan?

lecons.titre: 1. الفعل والفاعل - The Verb and Its Agent
lecons.explication:
In a verbal sentence, the فِعْل (verb) comes first, followed by the فَاعِل — the one who performs the action. The فاعل is always in the مرفوع case (nominative, marked by the damma ـُ).

Careful: فاعل does not mean 'actor' in the broad sense, but precisely 'the one who does the action of the preceding verb' — a grammatical role, not a profession.

exemples.sens: the student wrote — الطالبُ is فاعل, مرفوع

lecons.titre: 2. المفعول به - The Direct Object
lecons.explication:
What the action of the verb falls upon is called the مَفْعُول بِه. It takes the مَنْصُوب case (accusative), marked by the fatha ـَ (or the tanwin فتح ـً if indefinite).

A complete verbal sentence therefore follows the order: فعل (verb) + فاعل (agent, مرفوع) + مفعول به (object, منصوب).

exemples.sens: the student wrote the lesson — الدرسَ is مفعول به, منصوب
Fatima read a book — كتابًا is an indefinite مفعول به, tanwin fatḥ

lecons.titre: 1. المبني للمعلوم والمجهول - Active and Passive
lecons.explication: The passive is not formed by adding a word, but by changing the verb's internal vowels: the 1st vowel becomes a damma, the second-to-last a kasra. The فاعل disappears from the sentence — who performed the action is no longer stated.

exemples.sens: he wrote (active — المعلوم)
it was written (passive — المجهول)

lecons.titre: 2. نَائِب الفاعل - The Substitute Subject
lecons.explication: In the passive, the مفعول به (object of the active sentence) becomes نَائِب الفاعل — literally 'the one who replaces the subject'. It then takes the place of the فاعل and switches to the مرفوع case (nominative), whereas it was منصوب in the active.

exemples.sens: the student wrote the lesson (active)
the lesson was written — الدرسُ is نائب الفاعل, مرفوع

lecons.titre: 1. الإضافة - The Annexation (Possession by Juxtaposition)
lecons.explication: Arabic has no word for 'of': to say 'the student's book', the two nouns are simply juxtaposed. The first (مُضَاف) loses its الـ and its tanwin; the second (مُضَاف إِلَيْه) takes the مجرور case (kasra).

exemples.sens: the student's book (lit. 'book-of the-student')
the teacher's house

lecons.titre: 2. ضمائر الملكية المتصلة - Attached Possessive Suffixes
lecons.explication: To say 'my', 'your', 'his'..., Arabic attaches a suffix directly to the end of the noun, rather than using a separate word.

exemples.sens: my book
your book (to a man)
your book (to a woman)
his book
her book
our book

textes.titre: ٦. البَحْثُ عَنِ الطَّرِيقِ - Finding One's Way

lignes.arabe: السَّلَامُ عَلَيْكُمْ! عَفْوًا، أَيْنَ يَقَعُ المَسْجِدُ الكَبِيرُ؟
lignes.traduction: Peace be upon you! Excuse me, where is the big mosque?

lignes.arabe: وَعَلَيْكُمُ السَّلَامُ. اِمْشِ إِلَى الأَمَامِ، ثُمَّ اِنْعَطِفْ يَمِينًا عِنْدَ البَنْكِ.
lignes.traduction: And peace be upon you. Walk straight ahead, then turn right at the bank.
Is it far from here?

lignes.arabe: لَا، هُوَ قَرِيبٌ. حَوَالَيْ خَمْسِ دَقَائِقَ سَيْرًا عَلَى الأَقْدَامِ.
lignes.traduction: No, it's close. About five minutes on foot.

lignes.arabe: هَلْ أَحْتَاجُ إِلَى الِانْعِطَافِ مَرَّةً أُخْرَى؟
lignes.traduction: Do I need to turn again?

lignes.arabe: نَعَمْ، بَعْدَ البَنْكِ، اِنْعَطِفْ يَسَارًا، وَسَتَرَى المَسْجِدَ أَمَامَكَ مُبَاشَرَةً.
lignes.traduction: Yes, after the bank, turn left, and you'll see the mosque right in front of you.
Thank you very much for your help!
You're welcome, goodbye!

textes.titre: ٧. عَائِلَةٌ تُخَطِّطُ لِمُسْتَقْبَلِهَا - A Family Planning Its Future

lignes.arabe: السَّيِّدُ إِبْرَاهِيمُ رَجُلٌ حَكِيمٌ يَعِيشُ مَعَ عَائِلَتِهِ فِي مَدِينَةٍ كَبِيرَةٍ.
lignes.traduction: Mr. Ibrahim is a wise man who lives with his family in a big city.

lignes.arabe: عِنْدَهُ زَوْجَةٌ وَأَرْبَعَةُ أَوْلَادٍ: وَلَدَانِ وَبِنْتَانِ.
lignes.traduction: He has a wife and four children: two sons and two daughters.

lignes.arabe: كُلَّ سَنَةٍ، يَحْسُبُ السَّيِّدُ إِبْرَاهِيمُ زَكَاةَ مَالِهِ بِعِنَايَةٍ.
lignes.traduction: Every year, Mr. Ibrahim carefully calculates the Zakat on his wealth.

lignes.arabe: يَقُولُ لِأَوْلَادِهِ: «الزَّكَاةُ تُطَهِّرُ المَالَ، وَتُسَاعِدُ الفُقَرَاءَ وَالمَسَاكِينَ».
lignes.traduction: He tells his children: 'Zakat purifies wealth, and helps the poor and the needy.'

lignes.arabe: كَتَبَ السَّيِّدُ إِبْرَاهِيمُ وَصِيَّتَهُ أَيْضًا، لِأَنَّ الوَصِيَّةَ حَقٌّ عَلَى كُلِّ مُسْلِمٍ عِنْدَهُ مَالٌ.
lignes.traduction: Mr. Ibrahim also wrote his will, because the will is a right owed by every Muslim who has wealth.

lignes.arabe: هُوَ يَعْرِفُ أَنَّ الوَصِيَّةَ لَا تَتَجَاوَزُ ثُلُثَ المَالِ، وَلَا تَكُونُ لِوَارِثٍ.
lignes.traduction: He knows that the will cannot exceed a third of the wealth, and cannot go to an heir.

lignes.arabe: تَقُولُ زَوْجَتُهُ: «مِنَ المُهِمِّ أَنْ يَعْرِفَ أَوْلَادُنَا أَحْكَامَ المِيرَاثِ».
lignes.traduction: His wife says: 'It is important that our children know the rules of inheritance.'

lignes.arabe: يَجْتَمِعُ أَفْرَادُ العَائِلَةِ كُلَّ شَهْرٍ لِيَتَحَدَّثُوا عَنِ المَالِ وَالدِّينِ مَعًا.
lignes.traduction: The family members gather every month to talk about money and religion together.

lignes.arabe: يَقُولُ السَّيِّدُ إِبْرَاهِيمُ: «التَّخْطِيطُ اليَوْمَ يَحْمِي العَائِلَةَ غَدًا».
lignes.traduction: Mr. Ibrahim says: 'Planning today protects the family tomorrow.'

lignes.arabe: وَهَكَذَا، تَعِيشُ هَذِهِ العَائِلَةُ بِسَلَامٍ، لِأَنَّ كُلَّ فَرْدٍ يَعْرِفُ حُقُوقَهُ وَوَاجِبَاتِهِ.
lignes.traduction: And so, this family lives in peace, because every member knows their rights and duties.
In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.
All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds.
The Most Gracious, the Most Merciful,
Master of the Day of Judgment.
It is You we worship, and You we ask for help.
Guide us to the straight path,

lignes.arabe: صِرَاطَ الَّذِينَ أَنْعَمْتَ عَلَيْهِمْ غَيْرِ الْمَغْضُوبِ عَلَيْهِمْ وَلَا الضَّالِّينَ
lignes.traduction: the path of those You have blessed, not of those who have earned Your anger, nor of those who are astray.
In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

lignes.arabe: اللَّهُ لَا إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا هُوَ الْحَيُّ الْقَيُّومُ
lignes.traduction: Allah! There is no deity except Him, the Ever-Living, the Sustainer of existence.
Neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him.

lignes.arabe: لَهُ مَا فِي السَّمَاوَاتِ وَمَا فِي الْأَرْضِ
lignes.traduction: To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth.

lignes.arabe: مَنْ ذَا الَّذِي يَشْفَعُ عِنْدَهُ إِلَّا بِإِذْنِهِ
lignes.traduction: Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission?

lignes.arabe: وَسِعَ كُرْسِيُّهُ السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضَ وَلَا يَئُودُهُ حِفْظُهُمَا وَهُوَ الْعَلِيُّ الْعَظِيمُ
lignes.traduction: His Throne extends over the heavens and the earth, and their preservation tires Him not. He is the Most High, the Most Great. (Al-Baqarah, 255)

textes.titre: حَدِيث النِّيَّات - The Hadith of Intentions

lignes.traduction: Actions are but by intentions,
and every person will only have what they intended. (Sahih Al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim)

textes.titre: حَدِيث الأُخُوَّة - The Hadith of Brotherhood

lignes.arabe: لَا يُؤْمِنُ أَحَدُكُمْ حَتَّى يُحِبَّ لِأَخِيهِ مَا يُحِبُّ لِنَفْسِهِ
lignes.traduction: None of you truly believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself. (Sahih Al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim)

textes.titre: لِمَاذَا أُرْسِلَ الرَّسُولُ ﷺ - Why the Messenger Was Sent

lignes.traduction: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful
And We have not sent you, [O Muhammad], except as a mercy to the worlds. (Surah Al-Anbiya, verse 107)
In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful
Say: He is Allah, [who is] One.
Allah, the Eternal Refuge.
He neither begets nor is born.
Nor is there to Him any equivalent.

vocabulaire_nouveau.sens: the Eternal Refuge, He who depends on nothing

textes.titre: الاعْتِصَام بِحَبْل اللَّه - The Call to Unity

lignes.traduction: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

lignes.arabe: وَاعْتَصِمُوا بِحَبْلِ اللَّهِ جَمِيعًا وَلَا تَفَرَّقُوا
lignes.traduction: And hold firmly to the rope of Allah all together and do not become divided. (Surah Aal-'Imran, verse 103)

sciences_islamiques.sous_titre: Quran, Hadith, Sira, Tawhid, Fiqh — the great principles and the scholars' method, not just answers.
sciences_islamiques.avertissement: This module explicitly distinguishes what is agreed upon by consensus from what remains debated among scholars. Content prepared with the greatest care; a review by a qualified teacher is still recommended before any wide distribution.

lecons.titre: ١. أَوَّل آيَة نَزَلَتْ - The Very First Verse Revealed
lecons.explication: On this point, scholars are unanimous: it is a fact reported through an authentic chain of transmission (Sahih Al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, hadith of 'Aisha), which precisely describes the scene in the cave of Hira. No serious disagreement exists on this point — unlike the last verse, which we will see next.

exemples.sens: Read, in the name of your Lord who created (Surah Al-'Alaq, verses 1 to 5, revealed together in full)

lecons.titre: ٢. آخِر آيَة نَزَلَتْ - The Very Last Verse Revealed
lecons.explication:
Here, unlike the first verse, scholars do not agree on a single answer — and this is important to know: several candidate verses are reported through different chains of transmission, with none decisively prevailing. Two of the most cited opinions:

1) The verse on fearing the Day of Return (Al-Baqarah, 281), reported from Ibn 'Abbas.
2) The final verses on usurious interest (Ar-Riba), in the same surah.

Some commentators also cite the verse on the completion of religion (Al-Ma'idah, 3), but the majority point out that it was revealed during the Farewell Pilgrimage, some time before the very end — not literally last. Documenting this disagreement rather than artificially settling it is exactly the rigor that Quranic scholars have always applied.

Majority position: among these opinions, the one reported from Ibn 'Abbas (the verse Al-Baqarah 281) is the most widely transmitted in the great Tafsir compilations (At-Tabari, As-Suyuti), and it is the one most scholars consider most likely — without presenting this as absolute certainty, since the disagreement itself is authentically reported.

exemples.arabe: وَاتَّقُوا يَوْمًا تُرْجَعُونَ فِيهِ إِلَى اللَّهِ
exemples.translitteration: wattaqū yawman turja'ūna fīhi ila Allāh
exemples.sens: And fear a Day when you will be returned to Allah (Al-Baqarah, 281 — one of the most-reported opinions)

lecons.titre: ٣. المَكِّي وَالمَدَنِي - The Meccan / Medinan Classification
lecons.explication:
Surahs are classified by place (not simply date) of revelation: مَكِّي (Meccan) refers to what was revealed before the Hijrah (even outside Mecca), مَدَنِي (Medinan) to what was revealed after. According to the most widespread traditional classification: 86 Meccan surahs and 28 Medinan ones, for a total of 114.

This classification is more than a curiosity: it directly explains the style. Meccan surahs, shorter, focus on Tawhid and the afterlife; Medinan ones, longer, detail law and communal life — consistent with the circumstances of the young Muslim community at each period.

lecons.titre: ٤. الأَجْزَاء وَالأَحْزَاب - The Major Subdivisions of the Quran
lecons.explication:
The Quran is divided into reading units that did not exist during the Prophet's ﷺ lifetime, added later to facilitate regular recitation — a concrete example of organizational rigor, not of revelation.

جُزْء (Juz', plural أَجْزَاء): 30 equal parts, allowing the Quran to be completed in one month — the classical practice during Ramadan.
حِزْب (Hizb, plural أَحْزَاب): each Juz' is divided into 2 Ahzab, for 60 in total.
Each Hizb is divided into 4 quarters: رُبْع (a quarter), نِصْف (half the Hizb), then ثَلَاثَة أَرْبَاع (three quarters) — markers printed in the margin of most Mushaf copies, notably the Madinah Mushaf.

lecons.titre: ٥. الحُرُوف المُقَطَّعَة - The Disjointed Letters
lecons.explication:
29 surahs open with one or more isolated letters, pronounced separately (such as الم، حم، ن، كهيعص), using 14 of the 28 letters of the alphabet. Their exact meaning is among the questions scholars classify under مُتَشَابِه (the ambiguous), and two main positions are reported:

1) Some of the Salaf (including reports from Abu Bakr and 'Umar) held that only Allah knows their true meaning — a position of caution in the face of the unknown.
2) Other commentators see in them a reminder of the challenge issued to the Arabs: these letters, the simplest and most familiar in their language, nevertheless make up a text they are unable to imitate — a sign of the Quran's inimitability (Al-I'jaz).

Here again, both views are transmitted side by side in the great Tafsir works, with neither presented as definitively settled.

Majority position: the dominant position among most scholars, that of Tafwid ('we leave the true meaning to Allah, without stating an opinion on it'), remains the most cautious and most widely taught. It does not exclude the other reading: many scholars hold both at once — not knowing the exact meaning while still recognizing the sign of inimitability these letters represent.

exemples.sens: opening of Surah Al-Baqarah and two other surahs
opening of Surah Maryam — the longest combination (5 letters)

lecons.titre: ٦. البَسْمَلَة وَسُورَة التَّوْبَة - The Count of the Basmalah and the Special Case of At-Tawbah
lecons.explication:
The Basmalah opens 113 of the 114 surahs — it is absent from Surah At-Tawbah (the 9th). But it appears once more INSIDE the text, in Surah An-Naml (27, verse 30), quoted in Solomon's letter to the Queen of Sheba. Total: 113 + 1 = 114 occurrences, a figure scholars have always highlighted as echoing the number of surahs.

Why doesn't At-Tawbah have one? Two explanations are reported, without absolute settled certainty:

1) 'Uthman, who oversaw the compilation of the Mushaf, was not certain whether At-Tawbah was a standalone surah rather than a continuation of Al-Anfal (very similar themes) — out of caution, no Basmalah was inserted between the two so as not to settle an uncertain question.
2) The Basmalah expresses mercy and safety; yet At-Tawbah opens with a declaration of severance (Bara'ah) against those who violated their covenants — a tone that would not fit the usual opening.

exemples.arabe: إِنَّهُ مِنْ سُلَيْمَانَ وَإِنَّهُ بِسْمِ اللَّهِ الرَّحْمَٰنِ الرَّحِيمِ
exemples.translitteration: innahu min sulaymāna wa-innahu bismillāhi ar-raḥmāni ar-raḥīm
exemples.sens: 'It is from Solomon, and it is: In the name of Allah...' (An-Naml, 30 — the 'extra' Basmalah)

lecons.titre: ٧. خَصَائِص أُخْرَى - Other Notable Facts
lecons.explication:
A few additional facts that every university course in Quranic sciences covers early on:

The longest surah is Al-Baqarah (286 verses); the shortest, Al-Kawthar (only 3 verses). The longest verse in the Quran is the 'verse of debt' (Al-Baqarah, 282). Ayat Al-Kursi (Al-Baqarah, 255) is reported in an authentic hadith as the noblest verse of the Quran.

Regarding the total number of verses, rigor requires some nuance: the most widespread figure today is 6236 (Kufic count, used by the Madinah Mushaf), but the Basran, Syrian, or Meccan recitation traditions give slightly different counts (6204, 6214, 6219...). This is not a contradiction in the text itself, but in how certain long verses are divided into units — a matter of method, not of content.

lecons.titre: ٨. عِلْمُ التَّجْوِيد - What Is Tajwid?
lecons.explication:
التَّجْوِيد literally means 'to improve, to beautify'. Technically, it is the science that gives each letter its due right (Haqq al-Harf) and its merit (Mustahaqq al-Harf): pronouncing each sound from its exact articulation point, with its own characteristics, neither added to nor subtracted from.

The Quran itself commands this measured, articulated recitation. As for its ruling: learning the theoretical rules of Tajwid is a collective obligation (Fard Kifayah — if some in the community master it, the others are not at fault); however, APPLYING these rules while reciting is an individual obligation (Fard 'Ayn) for anyone reciting the Quran, since avoiding gross pronunciation errors (Lahn Jaliyy, which change the meaning) is a matter of respect owed to the revealed text.

⚠️ As noted elsewhere in this module: the written description provides guidance, it never replaces oral instruction with a qualified reciter (Shaykh or Shaykha), especially for the ear.

exemples.sens: And recite the Quran with measured recitation (Surah Al-Muzzammil, v.4) — the Quranic foundation of Tajwid

lecons.titre: ٩. مَخَارِجُ الحُرُوف - The Points of Articulation
lecons.explication:
Every Arabic letter has a precise Makhraj (articulation point). Scholars classically group them into five main zones, from the inside to the outside of the mouth:

1) الجَوْف (Al-Jawf, the mouth and throat cavity): the three long vowels (ا، و، ي), which have no precise contact point but resonate through the entire vocal tract.
2) الحَلْق (Al-Halq, the throat): ء ه (deep throat); ع ح (middle); غ خ (near the mouth).
3) اللِّسَان (Al-Lisan, the tongue): the vast majority of letters — including ق، ك (root of the tongue), ج ش ي (middle), ص س ز، ض، ل ن ر، ط د ت، ظ ذ ث (tip of the tongue against the teeth).
4) الشَّفَتَان (Ash-Shafatan, the two lips): ف (lower lip/teeth), ب م و (both lips).
5) الخَيْشُوم (Al-Khaysham, the nasal cavity): the nasal resonance (Al-Ghunnah) that accompanies the Nun and the Mim in certain situations — see the next two lessons.

lecons.titre: ١٠. أَحْكَامُ النُّونِ السَّاكِنَةِ وَالتَّنْوِين - The 4 Rules of the Silent Nun
lecons.explication:
When a vowelless Nun (نْ) or a Tanwin (ـً ـٍ ـٌ) meets the following letter, four treatments are possible depending on that letter:

1) الإِظْهَار (Al-Idhhar, clarity): before the 6 throat letters (ء ه ع ح غ خ) — the Nun is pronounced clearly, with no merging.
2) الإِدْغَام (Al-Idgham, merging): before the 6 letters يرملون — merging with Ghunnah (nasal resonance) for ي ن م و; merging without Ghunnah for ل ر.
3) الإِقْلَاب (Al-Iqlab, conversion): before the single letter ب — the Nun turns into a light Mim with Ghunnah, before pronouncing the Ba'.
4) الإِخْفَاء (Al-Ikhfa', concealment): before the remaining 15 letters — the sound is pronounced 'in between', neither fully clear nor fully merged, with Ghunnah.

exemples.sens: Idhhar — the silent Nun stays clear before the Hamza (Surah Al-Baqarah, v.62, illustrative example)
Idgham with full merging — the Nun disappears into the Ra' (classic illustrative example)
Iqlab — the Nun is pronounced as a light Mim before the Ba' (Surah Al-Baqarah, v.27, illustrative example)
Ikhfa' — the Nun's sound is concealed with nasal resonance before the Dhal (classic illustrative example)

lecons.titre: ١١. أَحْكَامُ الْمِيمِ السَّاكِنَة - The 3 Rules of the Silent Mim
lecons.explication:
The vowelless Mim (مْ) follows a similar logic, but with only three possible treatments:

1) الإِخْفَاءُ الشَّفَوِيّ (Ikhfa' Shafawi): before a Ba' (ب) — concealment with Ghunnah, lips lightly closed.
2) الإِدْغَامُ الشَّفَوِيّ (Idgham Shafawi): before another Mim (م) — full merging with Ghunnah.
3) الإِظْهَارُ الشَّفَوِيّ (Idhhar Shafawi): before the remaining 26 letters — clear pronunciation, with no merging or concealment (particular care before the Fa' and the Waw, whose articulation point is close).

lecons.titre: ١٢. القَلْقَلَة وَالمَدّ - Qalqalah and an Introduction to Madd
lecons.explication:
القَلْقَلَة (Al-Qalqalah) is a slight bouncing sound produced on 5 specific letters when they carry a Sukun (absence of a vowel): قطب جد — Qaf, Ta', Ba', Jim, Dal. It is more pronounced at the end of a verse (Qalqalah Kubra) than in the middle of a word (Qalqalah Sughra).

الْمَدّ (Al-Madd, elongation) concerns the three prolongation letters (ا، و، ي) when they follow a matching short vowel. A distinction is made between Madd Asli (natural, 2 beats — without it, the word becomes incomprehensible) and Madd Far'i (secondary, whose duration varies from 2 to 6 beats depending on the cause: meeting a Hamza, meeting a Sukun, etc.). The full detail of the Madd Far'i subcategories goes beyond this summary — that is exactly the subject matter of ongoing oral instruction.

exemples.sens: Qalqalah on the final Qaf (Sukun) — classic illustrative example
'al-'alamin' contains a Madd Asli (ا) — basic elongation of 2 beats

lecons.titre: ١٣. القِرَاءَاتُ العَشْر - The Ten Modes of Quranic Recitation
lecons.explication:
The Quran was revealed according to several authentic modes of recitation (Ahruf/Qira'at), all tracing back to the Prophet ﷺ through rigorous chains of transmission — these are not variations in meaning, but different ways of pronouncing, elongating, or sometimes vocalizing certain words of the same text.

Scholars classically recognize TEN of them, grouped into 'the Seven' (السَّبْعَة, fixed as canonical by Ibn Mujahid, d. 324H) and then 'the Three Completing Ones' (الثَّلَاثَة المُتَمِّمَة لِلْعَشَرَة):

THE SEVEN: 1) Nafi' (Madinah) — via Warsh and Qalun. 2) Ibn Kathir (Mecca). 3) Abu 'Amr (Basra). 4) Ibn 'Amir (Damascus). 5) 'Asim (Kufa) — via Hafs and Shu'bah. 6) Hamzah (Kufa). 7) Al-Kisa'i (Kufa).

THE THREE COMPLETING ONES: 8) Abu Ja'far (Madinah). 9) Ya'qub (Basra). 10) Khalaf (Kufa).

Each reader (Qari') generally transmits his recitation through TWO main transmitters (Rawi), hence compound names like 'Hafs 'an 'Asim' (Hafs, according to 'Asim).

lecons.titre: ١٤. أَشْهَرُ رِوَايَتَيْنِ - The Two Most Widespread Recitations Today
lecons.explication:
Of the ten, two transmissions dominate very widely across the contemporary Muslim world:

• Hafs 'an 'Asim: by far the most widespread worldwide — it is the one printed in almost all current Mushaf copies in the Middle East, Asia, and increasingly everywhere else.
• Warsh 'an Nafi': historically the most widely taught recitation in North and West Africa — including the Sahel — where it remains transmitted in many traditional Quranic schools, even though the Mushaf printed according to Hafs has also spread widely over time.

Among the best-known differences between these two recitations: the length of certain Madd (Warsh elongates certain cases further, up to 6 beats where Hafs marks 2 or 4) and, in a few specific words, a different vocalization — for example, in verse 4 of Al-Fatiha, Hafs reads 'مَالِكِ' (Maliki, 'Master'), while some of the other transmitted recitations read 'مَلِكِ' (Maliki, 'King'), both meanings being fully compatible and both mentioned elsewhere in the Quran.

⚠️ These are differences in authenticated transmission, not doctrinal divergences: no recitation is 'more true' than another. Their practice, like Tajwid, remains knowledge passed down orally by a qualified teacher in the recitation concerned.

exemples.sens: Hafs 'an 'Asim's recitation — 'Master of the Day of Judgment' (Al-Fatiha, v.4)

lecons.titre: ١٥. سُورَة النَّاس - Reading: The Very Last Surah of the Quran
lecons.explication: To close this course, a complete surah to read from start to finish: سُورَة النَّاس, the 114th and last of the Mushaf — a concrete conclusion after so much theory.

exemples.sens: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful
Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of mankind,
The King of mankind,
The God of mankind,
From the evil of the retreating whisperer [Satan]—
Who whispers [evil] into the breasts of mankind—
From among the jinn and mankind.

lecons.titre: ١. التصنيف الأساسي - Sahih, Hasan, Da'if, Mawdu'
lecons.explication:
Every hadith is classified according to a degree of reliability, never accepted wholesale without examination:

الصَّحِيح (Sahih, authentic): meets all the conditions of rigor (see the next lesson).
الحَسَن (Hasan, good): meets the same conditions, but with a narrator slightly less precise in memory — accepted as proof, one notch below Sahih.
الضَّعِيف (Da'if, weak): one of the conditions is missing — broken chain, unreliable narrator. Not used as proof in matters of belief or law.
المَوْضُوع (Mawdu', fabricated): purely invented and falsely attributed to the Prophet ﷺ. Hadith scholars devoted entire works (such as Al-Mawdu'at by Ibn Al-Jawzi) to cataloguing and exposing them — scientific rigor applied in its strictest form.

lecons.titre: ٢. شُرُوط الصِّحَّة - The 5 Conditions of an Authentic Hadith
lecons.explication:
For a hadith to be declared Sahih, five conditions must all be met — the absence of even one is enough to disqualify it:

1) اتِّصَال السَّنَد (Chain continuity): each narrator actually met and directly heard from the one before him, with no break.
2) عَدَالَة الرُّوَاة (Integrity of the narrators): each narrator is Muslim, of legal age, sound of mind, pious, avoiding major sins.
3) ضَبْط الرُّوَاة (Precision of the narrators): each narrator has a reliable memory (by heart or in writing), able to faithfully reproduce what he heard.
4) عَدَم الشُّذُوذ (Absence of irregularity): the report does not contradict a version transmitted through a more reliable chain.
5) عَدَم العِلَّة (Absence of hidden defect): no hidden flaw detected by specialists, even if the chain appears sound on the surface.

This level of rigor, systematically applied to tens of thousands of reports, is what sets the Islamic method of transmission apart from any other ancient oral tradition.

lecons.titre: ٣. السَّنَد وَالمَتْن - The Chain of Transmission
lecons.explication:
A complete hadith has two parts: السَّنَد (Sanad), the chain of narrators, and المَتْن (Matn), the text itself. One of the great hadith scholars, 'Abdullah ibn Al-Mubarak, summed up the importance of the Sanad this way: « الإسناد من الدين، ولولا الإسناد لقال من شاء ما شاء » — 'The chain of transmission is part of religion; without it, anyone could say whatever they wished.'

Here, as an example, is one of the chains considered by Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal to be the most reliable of all — known as « السِّلْسِلَة الذَّهَبِيَّة » (the Golden Chain):

chaine_isnad.note: Companion — heard directly from the Prophet ﷺ
Collected and transmitted this report in his Muwatta

lecons.titre: ٤. عِلْم الرِّجَال - The Biographical Science of Narrators
lecons.explication: To verify that a chain is reliable, scholars built an entire science devoted to the narrators themselves: dates of birth and death, places of residence, teachers studied under, reputation for memory and honesty. Biographical works thus catalogue tens of thousands of narrators, making it possible to verify, for example, that a given narrator could actually have met the person he claims to narrate a hadith from — and was not simply born after that person's death. This is a work of material verification, comparable to a systematic historical inquiry, carried out centuries before Western historical criticism formalized its methods.

lecons.titre: ٥. التَّصْنِيفُ بِعَدَدِ الرُّوَاة - Classification by Number of Narrators
lecons.explication:
Regardless of its degree of authenticity, a hadith is also classified according to the number of narrators at each generation of the chain:

المُتَوَاتِر (Al-Mutawatir): reported, at every generation, by a number of people so large that a secret agreement to fabricate a lie becomes materially impossible. This level provides absolute certainty (Yaqin) — a Mutawatir hadith can, by definition, never be weak. Hadiths at this level are few (scholars count several dozen, some compiled by As-Suyuti).

الآحَاد (Al-Ahad): everything else — reported by a number insufficient to reach the Mutawatir threshold, at at least one generation. This is the vast majority of the corpus, including most of the Sahih and Hasan hadiths in the Six Books. Ahad hadith is further subdivided:
• المَشْهُور (Al-Mashhur): three or more narrators at each generation, without reaching Tawatur.
• العَزِيز (Al-'Aziz): at least two narrators at a given generation.
• الغَرِيب (Al-Gharib): a single narrator at at least one generation — the most demanding to authenticate, since the slightest flaw in this sole narrator affects the entire hadith.

lecons.titre: ٦. عُيُوبُ اتِّصَالِ السَّنَد - Defects in Chain Continuity
lecons.explication:
Reminder: the first of the 5 conditions for Sahih is اتِّصَال السَّنَد (chain continuity, each narrator having actually met and heard from the one before him). When this continuity is broken, the hadith becomes Da'if — but the type of break itself has a precise name, since it does not always carry the same severity:

المُعَلَّق (Al-Mu'allaq): one or more narrators are missing at the START of the chain, on the compiler's side (for example when Al-Bukhari introduces a report with 'So-and-so said...' without tracing the full chain back).
المُرْسَل (Al-Mursal): a Tabi'i (successor, who did not meet the Prophet ﷺ) reports directly from the Prophet ﷺ, skipping the intermediate Companion.
المُعْضَل (Al-Mu'dal): two or more consecutive narrators are missing, anywhere in the chain.
المُنْقَطِع (Al-Munqati'): a single narrator is missing somewhere in the chain (outside the two ends already covered by Mu'allaq and Mursal) — or the chain contains an unidentified narrator (Mubham).

These four categories are classified as Da'if by default, but can sometimes be strengthened by independent chains that corroborate the same text — see the lesson on supporting evidence.

lecons.titre: ٧. عُيُوبٌ خَفِيَّة - Hidden Defects in the Sanad and the Matn
lecons.explication:
Beyond visible breaks in the chain, hadith science tracks more subtle flaws, in the chain (Sanad) as well as in the text (Matn):

الشَّاذّ (Ash-Shadhdh): a trustworthy narrator contradicts a group of narrators who are more reliable or more numerous than he is.
المُنْكَر (Al-Munkar): a weak narrator contradicts a reliable one — more serious than Shadhdh, since here the lone narrator does not himself have the required reliability.
المُدْرَج (Al-Mudraj): a narrator's comment or explanation ended up, through a transmission error, mixed into the hadith's own text, without distinction.
المَقْلُوب (Al-Maqlub): an inversion — a narrator's name swapped with another, or the order of certain words in the text reversed, generally due to a memorization error.
المُدَلَّس (Al-Mudallas): a narrator gives the impression of having heard directly from his teacher (through an ambiguous phrase like 'an' rather than 'haddathani', 'I heard from the mouth of') when this is not certain — hence the importance, in 'Ilm Ar-Rijal, of knowing which narrators are known for this practice (Mudallisun).
المَوْضُوع (Al-Mawdu'): reminder — purely fabricated (see lesson 1).

lecons.titre: ٨. الحَسَنُ لِغَيْرِهِ - How a Weak Hadith Can Be Strengthened
lecons.explication:
The Sahih/Hasan/Da'if classification is not always final for a hadith taken in isolation: the grading becomes more refined when looking at WHETHER other independent chains report the same content.

الصَّحِيح لِذَاتِهِ (Sahih li-Dhatihi): authentic in itself, meeting all 5 conditions on its own.
الحَسَن لِذَاتِهِ (Hasan li-Dhatihi): good in itself — same conditions, with a narrator slightly less precise in memory.
الصَّحِيح لِغَيْرِهِ (Sahih li-Ghayrihi): a Hasan hadith which, corroborated by one or more other independent chains of equal or greater strength, is RAISED to the rank of Sahih.
الحَسَن لِغَيْرِهِ (Hasan li-Ghayrihi): a Da'if hadith (for a minor reason, such as average memory — never for lying or fabrication) which, corroborated in the same way, is raised to the rank of Hasan.

This strengthening relies on two specific tools: المُتَابَعَة (Al-Mutaba'ah) — another chain reporting the SAME hadith, from the same Companion; الشَّاهِد (Ash-Shahid) — another chain reporting a hadith of SIMILAR meaning, but from a different Companion. This is the exact opposite of naive addition: several weak chains, weak for a MINOR reason, can together reach a level of proof that none reaches alone — but this never applies to a hadith that is Da'if Jiddan (very weak) or Mawdu'.

lecons.titre: ٩. الكُتُب السِّتَّة - The Six Great Collections
lecons.explication:
Two collections stand out for their degree of rigor: صَحِيح البُخَارِي (Sahih Al-Bukhari, by Imam Al-Bukhari, d. 256H) is considered by most Sunni scholars to be the most authentic book after the Quran itself. صَحِيح مُسْلِم (Sahih Muslim, by Imam Muslim ibn Al-Hajjaj, d. 261H) comes right after.

Together with four other collections (السُّنَن الأَرْبَعَة) — Abu Dawud, At-Tirmidhi, An-Nasa'i, and Ibn Majah — they form what is called الكُتُب السِّتَّة (the Six Books), the canonical reference for Sunni hadith. Some traditional lists substitute Ibn Majah with Imam Malik's Muwatta or the Sunan Ad-Darimi — a point of detail on which the compilers themselves documented their disagreement, without this affecting the core of the corpus.

lecons.titre: ١٠. الحَدِيث القُدْسِي - The Hadith Qudsi
lecons.explication: A category apart: the Hadith Qudsi reports a saying attributed to Allah, but phrased in the Prophet's ﷺ own words — unlike the Quran, which is the word of Allah word for word, recited in worship and inimitable in its very form. The Hadith Qudsi, on the other hand, can be Sahih, Hasan, or Da'if like any other hadith: the fact that it reports a divine saying does not exempt it from the rigorous examination of its chain.

exemples.arabe: يَا عِبَادِي إِنِّي حَرَّمْتُ الظُّلْمَ عَلَى نَفْسِي وَجَعَلْتُهُ بَيْنَكُمْ مُحَرَّمًا فَلَا تَظَالَمُوا
exemples.translitteration: yā 'ibādī innī ḥarramtu aẓ-ẓulma 'alā nafsī wa ja'altuhu baynakum muḥarraman falā taẓālamū
exemples.sens: O My servants, I have forbidden injustice for Myself, and I have made it forbidden among you — so do not wrong one another (reported in Sahih Muslim)

lecons.titre: ١١. حَدِيث صَحِيح - Reading: An Authentic Hadith to Close
lecons.explication: To close this course, one of the best-known hadiths in the entire corpus — reported by both Al-Bukhari and Muslim, therefore at the highest degree of authenticity, and placed at the opening of many collections because it is considered so fundamental.

exemples.arabe: إِنَّمَا الْأَعْمَالُ بِالنِّيَّاتِ، وَإِنَّمَا لِكُلِّ امْرِئٍ مَا نَوَى
exemples.translitteration: innamā al-a'mālu bin-niyyāti, wa innamā li-kulli imri'in mā nawā
exemples.sens: Actions are but by intentions, and every person will only have what they intended (Sahih Al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim)

lecons.titre: ١. عِلْم السِّيرَة - A Science, Not a Legend
lecons.explication: The Sira is not a collection of randomly transmitted anecdotes: it applies the same critical rigor as hadith science. Each biographical account is examined according to its chain of transmission, cross-checked against the Quran and authenticated hadiths, and specialists (such as Ibn Kathir in Al-Bidayah wan-Nihayah) explicitly weed out weak or legendary accounts that have sometimes crept into certain popular compilations — exactly the same verification work as in 'Ilm Al-Hadith, applied this time to an entire lifetime.

lecons.titre: ٢. خَط زَمَنِي - Timeline of the Major Events
lecons.explication: Eleven markers, from birth to death, to place each stage in time rather than learning isolated dates:

chronologie.evenement: Birth of the Prophet ﷺ in Mecca, the Year of the Elephant
First revelation (Surah Al-'Alaq), cave of Hira — age 40
Start of public preaching, after 3 years of private preaching
الهِجْرَة: emigration to Medina — start of the Islamic calendar
فَتْح مَكَّة: conquest of Mecca, with no major bloodshed
Death of the Prophet ﷺ in Medina, at age 63

lecons.titre: ٣. الأَمِين - Before the Revelation
lecons.explication: Born in Mecca into the clan of Banu Hashim (tribe of Quraysh), orphaned of his father before birth and then of his mother at age 6, he was raised by his grandfather 'Abd Al-Muttalib and then by his uncle Abu Talib. Long before the revelation, he was already known to all by the nickname الأَمِين ('the trustworthy one') for an honesty recognized even by his later opponents. He married Khadijah, a respected merchant, at age 25.

exemples.sens: the trustworthy one — the Prophet's ﷺ nickname even before the revelation

lecons.titre: ٤. مَوْلِدُهُ وَنَسَبُهُ - Birth, Parents, and Genealogy
lecons.explication:
Muhammad ﷺ was born in Mecca on Monday 12 Rabi' al-Awwal, in the year known as 'the Year of the Elephant' (around 570 CE) — the year Abrahah tried to destroy the Ka'bah with his elephants, an episode directly recounted in Surah Al-Fil.

His father, 'Abdullah ibn 'Abd Al-Muttalib, died before his birth: the Prophet ﷺ was thus born fatherless. His mother was Aminah bint Wahb, of the Zuhrah lineage. His paternal genealogy traces, father to son, back to 'Adnan, himself a descendant of Ishmael, son of Abraham — the paternal and maternal lines meet at their common ancestor Kilab ibn Murrah.

According to the reported account, as soon as he was born his mother sent word to his grandfather 'Abd Al-Muttalib, who came to carry him into the Ka'bah, invoked Allah for him, and named him Muhammad.

exemples.arabe: وَمُبَشِّرًا بِرَسُولٍ يَأْتِي مِن بَعْدِي اسْمُهُ أَحْمَدُ
exemples.sens: And bringing good tidings of a messenger to come after me, whose name is Ahmad (Surah As-Saff, v.6) — classically linked to the meaning of the Prophet's ﷺ name

lecons.titre: ٥. طُفُولَتُهُ - Childhood: Nursing, Orphanhood, Guardianship
lecons.explication:
According to the custom of Quraysh notables, infants were entrusted to Bedouin wet-nurses to grow up in the open desert air. This is how Halimah as-Sa'diyyah, of the Banu Sa'd tribe, nursed and raised him for two years, before keeping him a while longer at his mother's request — biographers report that she noticed a clear blessing in her household from the moment she took him in.

Around the age of five or six, his mother took him to Yathrib (future Medina) to visit his father's family. On the way back, she died at a place called Al-Abwa', between Mecca and Medina. Now orphaned of both father AND mother, he was taken in by his grandfather 'Abd Al-Muttalib, who himself died two years later (the Prophet ﷺ was then 8 years old) — entrusting his care, before dying, to his uncle Abu Talib, whom he knew to be tenderly attached to the child.

lecons.titre: ٦. رِحْلَةُ الشَّام وَبُحَيْرَا - The Journey to Syria and the Monk Bahira
lecons.explication: Around the age of twelve, he accompanied his uncle Abu Talib on a trading journey to Syria. In Busra, a Christian monk named Bahira, recognizing in him signs of prophethood foretold in the Scriptures — including the seal of prophethood between his shoulder blades — warned his uncle and advised him to quickly bring him back to Mecca, out of fear that the Jews of the region might harm him upon learning who he was.

lecons.titre: ٧. زَوَاجُهُ بِخَدِيجَة وَأَوْلَادُهُ - His Marriage to Khadijah and His Children
lecons.explication:
Known in Mecca for her honesty and integrity, Khadijah bint Khuwaylid — a wealthy merchant, twice widowed — entrusted him with managing her trading caravans. Won over by his legendary honesty, she proposed marriage to him through a friend. He was then 25, she about 40.

This union produced six children: two sons, Al-Qasim and 'Abdullah (both died in infancy — the second also known as At-Tayyib or At-Tahir in various accounts), and four daughters: Zaynab, Ruqayyah, Umm Kulthum, and Fatimah, the only one to leave descendants that continue on. Much later, in Medina, a seventh child — Ibrahim — was born to Mariyah al-Qibtiyyah. Khadijah remained his only wife until her death; his later marriages all took place after her, mostly in Medina.

lecons.titre: ٨. الوَحْي - The Revelation and the Secret Preaching
lecons.explication: At age 40, in the cave of Hira where he had taken to withdrawing, he received the first revelation. Three years of discreet preaching followed, limited to his close circle, before the command came to announce the message publicly — a period of preparation, not of hesitation.

lecons.titre: ٩. الإِسْرَاء وَالمِعْرَاج - The Night Journey and the Establishment of the Five Prayers
lecons.explication:
In year 10 of the prophetic mission, the Prophet ﷺ lost, one after another, his protective uncle Abu Talib and his wife Khadijah — a period so trying it is known as 'the Year of Sorrow' ('Am Al-Huzn). He then went to Ta'if seeking the support of the tribe of Thaqif, who rejected him with hostility even harsher than that of Quraysh.

It is in this context that Al-Isra' wal-Mi'raj takes place: the Prophet ﷺ is transported by night from the Sacred Mosque in Mecca to Al-Aqsa Mosque (Jerusalem), then raised through the heavens. It was during this journey that the five daily prayers were established — fifty at first, reduced to five after he repeatedly asked Allah for relief, while retaining the reward of fifty.

exemples.arabe: سُبْحَانَ الَّذِي أَسْرَىٰ بِعَبْدِهِ لَيْلًا مِّنَ الْمَسْجِدِ الْحَرَامِ إِلَى الْمَسْجِدِ الْأَقْصَى
exemples.sens: Exalted is He who took His Servant by night from al-Masjid al-Haram to al-Masjid al-Aqsa (Surah Al-Isra, v.1)

lecons.titre: ١٠. الهِجْرَة - The Emigration, a Turning Point
lecons.explication: Faced with growing persecution in Mecca, the emigration to Medina in 622 marks more than a geographic move: it is where the first organized Muslim community, with its own institutions, was built. This event is so foundational that it becomes the starting point of the Islamic calendar itself — every Hijri date is counted from that year.

lecons.titre: ١١. تَشْرِيعَاتُ المَدِينَة - The Establishment of Fasting, Zakat, and Hajj
lecons.explication:
Unlike the five prayers (established in Mecca, before the Hijrah), the other practical pillars of Islam were legislated in Medina, in the years following the community's settlement there:

• الصِّيَام (fasting during Ramadan) was made obligatory in year 2 of the Hijrah (622+2=624), the same year as the accompanying Zakat Al-Fitr.
• الزَّكَاة (the obligatory alms), in its codified form with precise thresholds and rates, was also detailed and made universal in Medina, largely during the same period — even though the general call to give charity and purify one's wealth was already present in the Meccan revelations.
• الحَجّ (the pilgrimage) was made obligatory later, around year 9 of the Hijrah. The Prophet ﷺ would perform only one Hajj in his lifetime as the Messenger establishing the definitive rites: حَجَّة الوَدَاع (the Farewell Pilgrimage), in year 10 of the Hijrah — during which he delivered a now-famous sermon on the equality of believers, just months before his death.

This sequencing — spiritual pillars first (Shahadah, Salah), then communal and social pillars afterward (Zakat, Sawm, Hajj), once the Muslim community was organized in Medina — reflects, according to biographers, a gradual pedagogy in Islamic legislation.

lecons.titre: ١٢. فَتْح مَكَّة - The Conquest of Mecca
lecons.explication: In year 8 of the Hijrah, Mecca was retaken with no major bloodshed. The Prophet ﷺ granted a general amnesty to those who had fought and persecuted him for over a decade — a gesture whose deliberately merciful nature, the opposite of revenge, biographers consistently emphasize.

lecons.titre: ١٣. وَفَاتُهُ ﷺ - His Death
lecons.explication: After the Farewell Pilgrimage in year 10 of the Hijrah — during which he delivered a now-famous sermon on the equality of believers — the Prophet ﷺ passed away in Medina the following year, at age 63, leaving behind an already organized community and a message recorded with painstaking care, as we have seen throughout this course.

lecons.titre: ١٤. نَص لِلقِرَاءَة - Reading: A Verse That Sums Up His Mission
lecons.explication: To close this course, a Quranic verse cited by every biographer at the opening or conclusion of their study, so well does it sum up the very meaning of the prophetic mission.

exemples.sens: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

exemples.translitteration: wa mā arsalnāka illā raḥmatan lil-'ālamīn
exemples.sens: And We have not sent you, [O Muhammad], except as a mercy to the worlds (Surah Al-Anbiya, verse 107)

etapes.titre: 3b. الخُلَفَاءُ الرَّاشِدُونَ - The Rightly Guided Caliphs
etapes.source: Sources islamiques/Université madina/tome_4/tome_4_histoire_des_califes.pdf — content directly adapted from this manual (quotations from Ibn Kathir, At-Tabari, Al-Baghdadi reproduced as referenced by the source).

lecons.titre: ١. الخُلَفَاءُ الرَّاشِدُون - The Four Rightly Guided Caliphs: Overview
lecons.explication:
Upon the death of the Prophet ﷺ in year 11H, the community appointed four successive caliphs — all among his closest companions, all promised Paradise during his lifetime: Abu Bakr As-Siddiq (11-13H), 'Umar ibn Al-Khattab (13-23H), 'Uthman ibn 'Affan (23-35H), and 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (35-40H). This period, called 'Al-Khilafah Ar-Rashidah', lasted about thirty years.

A point emphasized by biographers: none of the four seized power by force. Each acceded to the caliphate through a form of Shura (consultation) followed by a Bay'ah (public allegiance) — and once allegiance was given, breaking it was legitimate only in the case of manifest, established disbelief.

lecons.titre: ٢. أَبُو بَكْرٍ الصِّدِّيق - Abu Bakr: Unity Restored
lecons.explication:
The first caliph, he earned the title As-Siddiq ('the truthful one') for having believed without hesitation in the account of the Night Journey (Al-Isra') when others doubted it.

His caliphate is marked by the Ridda Wars: after the Prophet's ﷺ death, several Arab tribes renounced Islam or refused to pay Zakat. Facing this, Abu Bakr took a now-famous stand: 'By Allah, I will fight whoever separates prayer from Zakat' — refusing any concession on this pillar, even against those willing to pray while withholding the obligatory alms.

It was also under his caliphate, on 'Umar's suggestion after heavy losses among Quran reciters during these wars, that the first official compilation of the Quran into a single volume (Al-Mushaf) began, entrusted to Zayd ibn Thabit. Abu Bakr died after two years as caliph.

lecons.titre: ٣. عُمَرُ بْنُ الخَطَّاب - 'Umar: Organizing the State
lecons.explication:
The second caliph, nicknamed Al-Faruq ('he who distinguishes truth from falsehood'). His ten-year caliphate saw considerable territorial expansion — Persia, large parts of Byzantine lands — accompanied by extensive administrative organization of the emerging state (the Hijri calendar, the diwan for stipends, judicial institutions).
