He was assassinated by Abu Lu'lu'ah (Firuz), a slave of Persian origin, while leading the dawn prayer — closing out a caliphate biographers present as one of the most formative for the emerging Islamic state.

lecons.titre: ٤. عُثْمَانُ بْنُ عَفَّان - 'Uthman: Unifying the Quran
lecons.explication:
The third caliph, twice a son-in-law of the Prophet ﷺ (having successively married two of his daughters, hence his nickname Dhun-Nurayn, 'the man of two lights'). Under his caliphate, Muslim conquests reached as far as Tashkent in the east and a large part of North Africa in the west.

His most lasting contribution: faced with reading variations beginning to appear in the outlying provinces, he had a single official version of the Quran established (Al-Mushaf Al-'Uthmani), sent to the major cities of the empire — the reference text still used today.

His caliphate ended in a fitna (discord): insurgents, exploiting rumors and local political grievances, besieged his house in Medina and assassinated him. The source text notes that no Companion or their children took part in this killing — those responsible were outside elements, acting through instigation.

lecons.titre: ٥. عَلِيُّ بْنُ أَبِي طَالِب - 'Ali: The Last of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
lecons.explication:
Cousin of the Prophet ﷺ, husband of his daughter Fatimah, he was among the very first to embrace Islam — still a child, raised in the Prophet's ﷺ own household. He bore the nickname Abu Turab ('father of the earth'), given to him affectionately by the Prophet ﷺ himself.

Two episodes remain particularly associated with his courage: the night of the Hijrah, when he slept in the Prophet's ﷺ bed to cover his departure, at risk to his own life; and the Battle of Khaybar, where the Prophet ﷺ entrusted him with the banner, declaring that Allah would grant victory by his hand.

After 'Uthman's assassination, the community, in complete confusion, pressed him to accept the caliphate — he hesitated, preferring an advisory role, before yielding to the Companions' insistence. His five-year caliphate was marked by two painful internal wars, detailed in the next two lessons, before his assassination by a Kharijite in year 40H.

lecons.titre: ٦. مَعْرَكَتَا الجَمَلِ وَصِفِّين - Two Internal Wars, One Contested Ijtihad
lecons.explication:
The Battle of the Camel (36H): 'A'ishah, accompanied by Talhah and Az-Zubayr, went to Basra with the declared intention of reconciling positions after 'Uthman's assassination — not to fight 'Ali. An agreement even seemed to have been reached between the two camps; but instigators of the fitna triggered a clash by night to sabotage the reconciliation. The fighting stopped when 'A'ishah's camel was brought down — hence the battle's name. 'Ali then had her escorted back to Mecca with full honors.

The Battle of Siffin (37H): pitting 'Ali against Mu'awiyah, governor of Syria, who refused to pledge allegiance until 'Uthman's killers were brought to justice — a disagreement over method ('Ali wanted to first consolidate his power before delivering justice), not a challenge to the caliphate itself. After six months of correspondence and attempted reconciliation, the fighting ended in an arbitration (At-Tahkim) proposed by 'Amr ibn Al-'As — but the arbitration failed to settle the matter, and each side returned to its territory with no definitive reconciliation.

Position reported by Sunni scholars (as cited by the source manual): both conflicts stemmed from a good-faith Ijtihad (effort of interpretation) on both sides, not from betrayal — 'whoever is right earns two rewards, whoever is mistaken earns one', according to the authentic hadith cited on this matter.

lecons.titre: ٧. نَشْأَةُ الخَوَارِج - The Birth of the Kharijites
lecons.explication:
It was out of the failed Siffin arbitration that a group emerged rejecting both the decision and 'Ali's authority itself: الخَوَارِج (the Kharijites, literally 'those who went out' — of obedience to the legitimate imam).

'Ali first attempted dialogue: he sent Ibn 'Abbas to reason with them, which won back some of them. The rest persisted, descending into violence — looting, bloodshed, including the murder of a Companion, 'Abdullah ibn Khabbab, along with his wife. 'Ali then marched against them and decisively defeated them at the Battle of An-Nahrawan (37H, southeast of Baghdad).

It was a survivor of this movement, 'Abd Ar-Rahman ibn Muljam, who assassinated 'Ali three years later, in year 40H, believing this act would bring him closer to Allah.

Doctrine summarized by the source text (quoting Al-Baghdadi, 'Al-Farq bayn Al-Firaq'): the Kharijites agreed in declaring both 'Ali and 'Uthman disbelievers, along with anyone who approved of the arbitration or sided with it. Majority Sunni position, already noted in this course's Fiqh module: categorical rejection of this logic of sweeping takfir.

lecons.titre: ٨. جُذُورُ الافْتِرَاق - The Roots of Another Rift
lecons.explication:
Alongside the open conflict with the Kharijites, the source text mentions another shadowy actor behind several episodes of this troubled period: 'Abdullah ibn Saba' and his followers, described in the manual as instigators of the discord that precipitated the Battle of the Camel just as an agreement seemed close.

⚠️ Methodological caution note: this account, reported by several classical historians (including At-Tabari), is part of the version transmitted by the majority Sunni tradition regarding the origins of the party (Shi'ah, 'the partisans') that would later develop its own doctrine on the succession of the Prophet ﷺ (the Imamate). The figure and exact role of Ibn Saba' are debated among contemporary historians, including Sunni ones, as to their precise extent. This module reports the account as transmitted by the classical sources used, without settling a historiographical debate beyond the scope of an introductory course.

What Sunni tradition mainly retains from this period, beyond debates over its exact origins: the oldest and broadest division within the Ummah crystallized around the question of succession and legitimate authority after the Prophet ﷺ — a subject already addressed with the same caution in the Fiqh module (lesson on الشِّيعَة).

lecons.titre: ٩. عَامُ الجَمَاعَة - The Year Unity Was Restored (41H)
lecons.explication:
After 'Ali's assassination, Al-Hasan ibn 'Ali — his son — received allegiance in Iraq. Rather than prolong an already deadly civil war, he chose to cede the caliphate to Mu'awiyah in order to preserve the community's unity, thereby fulfilling a prophecy of the Prophet ﷺ reported by Al-Bukhari: 'This son of mine is a leader; perhaps Allah will reconcile through him two great groups of Muslims.'

Year 41H is thus called 'Am Al-Jama'ah (the Year of Unity) — the community regained a single caliph after the years of fitna. Biographers highlight Al-Hasan's gesture as a model of Islah (reconciliation) placed above personal ambition.

etapes.source: Al-Ussûl ath-Thalâtha (الأصول الثلاثة), Cheikh Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Wahhâb — texte fourni par l'utilisateur, traduction de référence.
etapes.avertissement_source: Ce parcours suit fidèlement la structure et les citations du traité original. La traduction française reprend celle fournie ; à faire valider par un enseignant qualifié avant diffusion large, comme pour tout contenu doctrinal de ce module.

sous_rubriques.description: The foundational course, as structured by Shaykh Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Wahhab.

lecons.titre: ٠. مَصْدَرُ هَذَا الدَّرْسِ - Where This Course Comes From
lecons.explication:
This course follows, step by step, a specific text rather than staying at generalities: 'Al-Ussul ath-Thalatha' (The Three Foundations), by Shaykh Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Wahhab (d. 1206H). It is one of the very first short 'Aqidah treatises taught across the Sunni world — cited, memorized, and commented on well beyond any single movement, in West Africa as elsewhere, for its economy of words and its rigorous construction from scriptural evidence rather than unsourced claims.

In fairness: citing a text's author is not a judgment on all his later positions or on any particular movement — it is simply the same rule of rigor this module already applies to Hadith (always trace back to the source). Every statement that follows is backed by an explicitly cited verse or hadith, exactly as the original text does.

lecons.titre: ١. أَرْبَعُ مَسَائِل - The Four Starting Obligations
lecons.explication:
The treatise opens with a four-part obligation, even before discussing belief: (1) العِلْم — knowledge: knowing Allah, knowing His Prophet ﷺ, knowing the religion of Islam with its proofs; (2) العَمَل — putting it into practice; (3) الدَّعْوَة — calling others to it; (4) الصَّبْر — patiently enduring the difficulties this may bring.

The order is deliberately pedagogical: knowledge precedes action (as Al-Bukhari recalls in his chapter 'Knowledge before speech and action'), since one cannot correctly act on what one does not know.

exemples.arabe: وَالْعَصْرِ * إِنَّ الْإِنسَانَ لَفِي خُسْرٍ * إِلَّا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا وَعَمِلُوا الصَّالِحَاتِ وَتَوَاصَوْا بِالْحَقِّ وَتَوَاصَوْا بِالصَّبْرِ
exemples.sens: By Time! Indeed mankind is in loss, except those who believe, do righteous deeds, and enjoin upon one another truth and enjoin upon one another patience. (Surah Al-'Asr, in full — cited by the author as the basis of the four obligations. Ash-Shafi'i is said to have remarked that if Allah had revealed only this surah, it would have sufficed for mankind.)

lecons.titre: ٢. ثَلَاثُ مَسَائِل - Three Things Every Muslim Must Know
lecons.explication:
Even before going into the detail of the Three Foundations, the text lays out three basic certainties, to be known AND put into practice:

1) Allah created us and granted us sustenance; He did not leave us without purpose — He sent us a Messenger. Whoever obeys him enters Paradise, whoever disobeys him enters the Fire.
2) Allah does not accept that anyone be associated with Him in worship — not even a close angel, not even a sent prophet.
3) Whoever obeys the Messenger and affirms Allah's oneness cannot take as allies those who openly oppose Allah and His Messenger, even if they are their closest relatives.

exemples.arabe: إِنَّا أَرْسَلْنَا إِلَيْكُمْ رَسُولًا شَاهِدًا عَلَيْكُمْ كَمَا أَرْسَلْنَا إِلَى فِرْعَوْنَ رَسُولًا
exemples.sens: Indeed, We have sent to you a Messenger as a witness over you, just as We sent to Pharaoh a messenger (Surah Al-Muzzammil, v.15)

exemples.arabe: وَأَنَّ الْمَسَاجِدَ لِلَّهِ فَلَا تَدْعُوا مَعَ اللَّهِ أَحَدًا
exemples.sens: And that the mosques are for Allah, so do not invoke anyone along with Allah (Surah Al-Jinn, v.18)

exemples.arabe: لَّا تَجِدُ قَوْمًا يُؤْمِنُونَ بِاللَّهِ وَالْيَوْمِ الْآخِرِ يُوَادُّونَ مَنْ حَادَّ اللَّهَ وَرَسُولَهُ وَلَوْ كَانُوا آبَاءَهُمْ
exemples.sens: You will not find a people who believe in Allah and the Last Day having affection for those who oppose Allah and His Messenger, even if they were their fathers (Surah Al-Mujadalah, v.22)

lecons.titre: ٣. الْحَنِيفِيَّة - The Pure Religion of Abraham
lecons.explication:
The text then defines the very purpose of creation: 'الحَنِيفِيَّة مِلَّة إِبْرَاهِيم' — the pure religion of Abraham — consists of worshiping Allah alone, devoting to Him exclusive and sincere worship. This is what Allah imposed on all of humanity, and it is the very reason for the creation of Jinn and Mankind.

'Worship Me' (يَعْبُدُونِ) is explained here as meaning 'affirm My oneness' (يُوَحِّدُونِ): worshiping Allah and affirming His oneness are one and the same. The greatest command is thus Tawhid (affirming Allah's oneness in worship), and the greatest prohibition is Shirk (associating anything else with Him in that worship).

exemples.arabe: وَمَا خَلَقْتُ الْجِنَّ وَالْإِنسَ إِلَّا لِيَعْبُدُونِ
exemples.sens: And I did not create the Jinn and Mankind except to worship Me (Surah Adh-Dhariyat, v.56)

exemples.arabe: وَاعْبُدُوا اللَّهَ وَلَا تُشْرِكُوا بِهِ شَيْئًا
exemples.sens: Worship Allah and associate nothing with Him (Surah An-Nisa, v.36)

lecons.titre: ٤. الأُصُولُ الثَّلَاثَة - The Three Foundations: Introduction
lecons.explication: Now comes the heart of the treatise — the three things every human being is obligated to know: that the servant know (1) his Lord, (2) his religion, and (3) his Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. The next three lessons unfold each of these three foundations with its proofs.

lecons.titre: ٥. الأَصْل الأَوَّل - First Foundation: Who Is Your Lord?
lecons.explication:
The text's answer: 'My Lord is Allah, who has nurtured me and the entire Universe through His favors. He is the One I worship; I worship none besides Him.' The Universe (Al-'Alamin) is everything that exists besides Allah — and the believer is himself part of it.

How was He known? 'Through His signs and His creation' — night and day, the sun and the moon on one hand; the seven heavens, the seven earths, and everything they contain on the other. Ibn Kathir sums it up: 'The One who created these things is [alone] worthy of worship' — Ar-Rabb (the Lord) is precisely Al-Ma'bud (the One who is worshiped).

exemples.sens: All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds (Surah Al-Fatiha, v.2)

exemples.arabe: وَمِنْ آيَاتِهِ اللَّيْلُ وَالنَّهَارُ وَالشَّمْسُ وَالْقَمَرُ لَا تَسْجُدُوا لِلشَّمْسِ وَلَا لِلْقَمَرِ وَاسْجُدُوا لِلَّهِ الَّذِي خَلَقَهُنَّ
exemples.sens: And of His signs are the night and day and the sun and moon. Do not prostrate to the sun or to the moon, but prostrate to Allah, who created them (Surah Fussilat, v.37)

exemples.arabe: يَا أَيُّهَا النَّاسُ اعْبُدُوا رَبَّكُمُ الَّذِي خَلَقَكُمْ وَالَّذِينَ مِن قَبْلِكُمْ لَعَلَّكُمْ تَتَّقُونَ
exemples.sens: O mankind! Worship your Lord, who created you and those before you, that you may become righteous (Surah Al-Baqarah, v.21)

lecons.titre: ٦. أَنْوَاعُ الْعِبَادَة - Forms of Worship Cited by the Text
lecons.explication:
The treatise then lists, each with its own Quranic proof, the forms of worship Allah commanded: Islam, Iman, Ihsan — and among the acts of the heart and body that fall under them: supplication (Ad-Du'a), fear (Al-Khawf), hope (Ar-Raja'), total reliance (At-Tawakkul), longing and dread (Ar-Raghbah wa Ar-Rahbah), humility (Al-Khushu'), reverent fear (Al-Khashyah), repentant return to Allah (Al-Inabah), seeking help, protection, and rescue (Al-Isti'anah, Al-Isti'adhah, Al-Istighathah), ritual sacrifice (Adh-Dhabh), and vows (An-Nadhr).

The principle uniting all of this, hammered home by the text: whoever directs even ONE of these forms of worship to someone other than Allah becomes, by that very act, one who commits Shirk (Mushrik).

exemples.sens: It is You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help (Surah Al-Fatiha, v.5)
And your Lord says: Call upon Me, I will respond to you (Surah Ghafir, v.60) — the basis of the hadith 'supplication is the essence of worship'

exemples.arabe: وَمَن يَدْعُ مَعَ اللَّهِ إِلَٰهًا آخَرَ لَا بُرْهَانَ لَهُ بِهِ
exemples.sens: And whoever invokes besides Allah another deity for which he has no proof — his account is only with his Lord (Surah Al-Mu'minun, v.117)

lecons.titre: ٧. الأَصْل الثَّانِي - Second Foundation: Religion in Three Levels
lecons.explication: Knowing the religion of Islam, the text says, means 'submitting to Allah through Tawhid, obeying Him in compliance, and disavowing Shirk and its followers'. This religion comprises three levels (Maratib), each with its own pillars: الإِسْلَام (Submission), الإِيمَان (Faith), الإِحْسَان (Excellence). The next three lessons detail each one.

lecons.titre: ٨. المَرْتَبَةُ الأُولَى: الإِسْلَام - First Level: The Five Pillars
lecons.explication:
The pillars of Islam are five: testifying that there is no deity worthy of worship except Allah and that Muhammad is His messenger; establishing prayer; paying Zakat; fasting Ramadan; and pilgrimage to the Sacred House for those able to do so.

The text explains the exact meaning of the twofold testimony: 'La ilaha' negates any deity worthy of worship besides Allah; 'illa Allah' affirms that He alone is, without partner — just as He has no partner in creation. Testifying that Muhammad is His messenger concretely implies: obeying him in what he commands, believing what he reports, avoiding what he forbids, and worshiping Allah only according to what he transmitted.

exemples.arabe: شَهِدَ اللَّهُ أَنَّهُ لَا إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا هُوَ وَالْمَلَائِكَةُ وَأُولُو الْعِلْمِ
exemples.sens: Allah bears witness that there is no deity except Him, and [so do] the angels and possessors of knowledge (Surah Aal 'Imran, v.18)

exemples.arabe: لَقَدْ جَاءَكُمْ رَسُولٌ مِّنْ أَنفُسِكُمْ عَزِيزٌ عَلَيْهِ مَا عَنِتُّمْ
exemples.sens: There has certainly come to you a Messenger from among yourselves; grievous to him is what you suffer (Surah At-Tawbah, v.128) — proof of the prophetic testimony

exemples.arabe: وَلِلَّهِ عَلَى النَّاسِ حِجُّ الْبَيْتِ مَنِ اسْتَطَاعَ إِلَيْهِ سَبِيلًا
exemples.sens: And [due] to Allah from the people is a pilgrimage to the House — for whoever is able to find a way (Surah Aal 'Imran, v.97)

lecons.titre: ٩. المَرْتَبَةُ الثَّانِيَة: الإِيمَان - Second Level: The Six Pillars
lecons.explication:
Faith (Al-Iman) has, according to the text, 'seventy-odd branches' (Shu'bah): the highest is saying 'La ilaha illa Allah', the most modest is removing a harmful object from a path — and modesty (Al-Haya') is a branch in its own right.

Its six pillars, reported in the famous Hadith of Jibril: believing in Allah, His angels, His Books, His messengers, the Last Day, and believing in destiny (Al-Qadar), whether favorable or unfavorable.

exemples.arabe: لَّيْسَ الْبِرَّ أَن تُوَلُّوا وُجُوهَكُمْ قِبَلَ الْمَشْرِقِ وَالْمَغْرِبِ وَلَٰكِنَّ الْبِرَّ مَنْ آمَنَ بِاللَّهِ وَالْيَوْمِ الْآخِرِ وَالْمَلَائِكَةِ وَالْكِتَابِ وَالنَّبِيِّينَ
exemples.sens: Righteousness is not that you turn your faces toward the East or the West, but righteousness is [in] one who believes in Allah, the Last Day, the angels, the Book, and the prophets (Surah Al-Baqarah, v.177)
Indeed, all things We created with predestination (Surah Al-Qamar, v.49) — proof regarding destiny

lecons.titre: ١٠. المَرْتَبَةُ الثَّالِثَة: الإِحْسَان - Third Level: A Single Pillar
lecons.explication:
Ihsan has only one pillar, defined by the Prophet ﷺ himself in the Hadith of Jibril: 'To worship Allah as though you see Him; and if you do not see Him, then indeed He sees you.'

This hadith is one of the most foundational in all religious science: an angel, in human form, questions the Prophet ﷺ in front of the Companions about Islam, Iman, Ihsan, and then the Hour — and the Prophet ﷺ later reveals that it was the angel Jibril, who had come to 'teach the religion' to the community. This is the reference text that structures the entire three-level framework seen in this course.

exemples.arabe: أَنْ تَعْبُدَ اللَّهَ كَأَنَّكَ تَرَاهُ، فَإِن لَّمْ تَكُن تَرَاهُ فَإِنَّهُ يَرَاكَ
exemples.sens: To worship Allah as though you see Him; and if you do not see Him, then indeed He sees you — the Prophet's ﷺ answer in the Hadith of Jibril (reported by Muslim, Kitab Al-Iman)

exemples.arabe: إِنَّ اللَّهَ مَعَ الَّذِينَ اتَّقَوا وَّالَّذِينَ هُم مُّحْسِنُونَ
exemples.sens: Indeed, Allah is with those who fear Him and those who are doers of good (Surah An-Nahl, v.128)

lecons.titre: ١١. الأَصْل الثَّالِث - Third Foundation: Knowing the Prophet ﷺ
lecons.explication:
Muhammad, son of 'Abdullah, son of 'Abd Al-Muttalib, son of Hashim — of the tribe of Quraysh, itself Arab, descended from Ishmael son of Abraham. He lived sixty-three years: forty before the revelation, twenty-three as prophet and messenger.

He was made a prophet through the revelation of 'Iqra'!' (Read!, Surah Al-'Alaq); he became a messenger with the revelation of Al-Muddaththir, sending him to warn against Shirk and call to Tawhid. His birthplace is Mecca; he emigrated to Medina.

exemples.arabe: يَا أَيُّهَا الْمُدَّثِّرُ * قُمْ فَأَنذِرْ * وَرَبَّكَ فَكَبِّرْ * وَثِيَابَكَ فَطَهِّرْ * وَالرُّجْزَ فَاهْجُرْ
exemples.sens: O you who covers himself [with a garment], arise and warn. And your Lord glorify. And your clothing purify. And uncleanliness avoid. (Surah Al-Muddaththir, v.1-5) — the investiture as messenger

lecons.titre: ١٢. عَشْرُ سِنِينَ ثُمَّ الإِسْرَاء - Ten Years of Preaching, Then the Mi'raj
lecons.explication: For ten years in Mecca, the Prophet ﷺ called solely to Tawhid. At the end of that decade, he was raised to the heavens (Al-Isra' wal-Mi'raj), and it was on this occasion that the five daily prayers were prescribed. He then prayed in Mecca for three more years, before receiving the command to emigrate to Medina.

lecons.titre: ١٣. الْهِجْرَة - The Emigration: Meaning and Obligation
lecons.explication: The Hijrah consists of leaving a land dominated by Shirk for a land of Islam. The text insists: this obligation remains valid for the community 'until the coming of the Hour' — for anyone unable to practice their religion where they are. An exception is explicitly made for those genuinely unable to do so (the weak, women, children with no means or way), whom Allah may forgive.

exemples.arabe: إِلَّا الْمُسْتَضْعَفِينَ مِنَ الرِّجَالِ وَالنِّسَاءِ وَالْوِلْدَانِ لَا يَسْتَطِيعُونَ حِيلَةً وَلَا يَهْتَدُونَ سَبِيلًا * فَأُولَٰئِكَ عَسَى اللَّهُ أَن يَعْفُوَ عَنْهُمْ
exemples.sens: Except for the oppressed among men, women, and children who cannot devise a plan nor are they directed to a way — for those it is expected that Allah will pardon them (Surah An-Nisa, v.98-99)

lecons.titre: ١٤. اسْتِقْرَارٌ فِي الْمَدِينَة - Medina: The Law Is Completed, the Mission Fulfilled
lecons.explication:
Once settled in Medina, the Prophet ﷺ received the command to establish the rest of Islamic legislation: Zakat, fasting, pilgrimage, Jihad, the call to prayer, enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong. He lived ten more years, then passed away — his religion, however, remains.

The text insists: he left nothing good without showing it to his community, and nothing evil without warning them of it. The good he pointed to is Tawhid and everything Allah loves; the evil he warned against is Shirk and everything Allah rejects.

exemples.arabe: الْيَوْمَ أَكْمَلْتُ لَكُمْ دِينَكُمْ وَأَتْمَمْتُ عَلَيْكُمْ نِعْمَتِي وَرَضِيتُ لَكُمُ الْإِسْلَامَ دِينًا
exemples.sens: This day I have perfected for you your religion and completed My favor upon you and have approved for you Islam as religion (Surah Al-Ma'idah, v.3)
Indeed, you will die, and indeed, they will die (Surah Az-Zumar, v.30) — proof of the Prophet's ﷺ death, cited in the text against any notion of immortality attributed to him

lecons.titre: ١٥. أَنْبِيَاءٌ مِن نُوحٍ إِلَى مُحَمَّدٍ - An Unbroken Chain of Messengers
lecons.explication: The text recalls that Allah sent a messenger to every community, from the first — Nuh (Noah) — to the last — Muhammad ﷺ, the Seal of the Prophets (Khatam an-Nabiyyin). Each came with the same core message: worship Allah alone and reject the Taghut. It is this common denominator, more than the diversity of detailed laws (Shara'i'), that constitutes the Tawhid transmitted throughout all of prophetic history.

exemples.arabe: وَلَقَدْ بَعَثْنَا فِي كُلِّ أُمَّةٍ رَّسُولًا أَنِ اعْبُدُوا اللَّهَ وَاجْتَنِبُوا الطَّاغُوتَ
exemples.sens: And We certainly sent into every community a messenger, [saying], 'Worship Allah and avoid Taghut' (Surah An-Nahl, v.36)

lecons.titre: ١٦. مَعْنَى الطَّاغُوت - The Taghut: What Opposes Tawhid
lecons.explication:
Ibn Al-Qayyim provides the definition adopted by the text: 'The Taghut is anything by which the servant oversteps his proper bounds — whether an object worshiped, followed, or obeyed [besides Allah].' The Tawaghit are numerous, but their leaders number five: Iblis; whoever accepts being worshiped; whoever calls people to worship him; whoever claims to possess some knowledge of the Unseen (Al-Ghayb); and whoever governs by other than what Allah has revealed.

It is precisely this dual movement — rejecting the Taghut AND believing in Allah — that constitutes, the text says, the true meaning of 'La ilaha illa Allah'.

exemples.arabe: لَا إِكْرَاهَ فِي الدِّينِ قَد تَّبَيَّنَ الرُّشْدُ مِنَ الْغَيِّ فَمَن يَكْفُرْ بِالطَّاغُوتِ وَيُؤْمِن بِاللَّهِ فَقَدِ اسْتَمْسَكَ بِالْعُرْوَةِ الْوُثْقَىٰ لَا انفِصَامَ لَهَا
exemples.sens: There is no compulsion in religion. The right course has become clear from the wrong. So whoever disbelieves in Taghut and believes in Allah has grasped the most trustworthy handhold with no break in it (Surah Al-Baqarah, v.256)

lecons.titre: ١٧. مُلَاحَظَةٌ تَكْمِيلِيَّة - A Useful Note for What Follows
lecons.explication:
The triad of Rububiyyah / Uluhiyyah / Asma' wa Sifat — often presented as THE classification of Tawhid — does not appear by name in this text, which deliberately remains simpler. This three-category systematization was mainly developed and popularized by Ibn Taymiyyah; other Sunni theological schools (Ash'ari, Maturidi) share the same Tawhid and reject the same Shirk, but traditionally organize their exposition differently. The substance is shared; the threefold division is just one pedagogical way among others of presenting it — useful to know before approaching other 'Aqidah manuals.

👉 A tab dedicated to this classification (Rububiyyah / Uluhiyyah / Asma' wa Sifat) is available just above — far more detailed than this brief aside.

lecons.titre: ١٨. نَص لِلقِرَاءَة - Closing Reading: The Surah Most Focused on Tawhid
lecons.explication: To close this course, the surah the Prophet ﷺ himself described as equivalent, on its own, to a third of the Quran, so concentrated is it on the question of Tawhid — سُورَة الإِخْلَاص.

exemples.sens: Say: He is Allah, [who is] One.
Allah, the Eternal Refuge.
He neither begets nor is born.
Nor is there to Him any equivalent. (Surah Al-Ikhlas, in full)

sous_rubriques.description: The threefold classification popularized by Ibn Taymiyyah — the same Tawhid, presented differently.

lecons.titre: ٠. لِمَاذَا هَذَا التَّقْسِيم؟ - Where Does This Classification Come From?
lecons.explication:
The previous tab follows 'Al-Ussul ath-Thalatha', a deliberately simple text, designed for a first introduction. Many believers also encounter — in classes, sermons, or other manuals — a second framework for reading Tawhid, in three categories: الرُّبُوبِيَّة (Rububiyyah), الأُلُوهِيَّة (Uluhiyyah), and الأَسْمَاء وَالصِّفَات (Asma' wa Sifat).

This precise systematization was mainly developed and popularized by Ibn Taymiyyah (d. 728H), notably in 'Al-'Aqidah Al-Wasitiyyah', and later widely adopted in contemporary teaching — to the point of being, for many today, the first thing that comes to mind on hearing the word 'Tawhid'. It in no way contradicts the Three Foundations: it is another way, more detailed on this specific point, of organizing the SAME doctrinal content (the first foundation, 'knowing your Lord', is here expanded into three parts).

Honesty required: other Sunni theological schools (Ash'ari, Maturidi) share the same Tawhid and reject the same Shirk, but do not necessarily use this precise threefold division, nor always the same method for the third part (Asma' wa Sifat) — see the nuance at the end of this course.

lecons.titre: ١. تَوْحِيدُ الرُّبُوبِيَّة - The Tawhid of Lordship
lecons.explication:
تَوْحِيد الرُّبُوبِيَّة: firmly believing that Allah alone creates, owns, and governs everything that exists — no partner in the act of creating, giving life, causing death, providing sustenance, or managing the universe.

An essential and often misunderstood point: this part alone is NOT ENOUGH to make someone a believer. The Quran explicitly reports that the polytheists contemporary with the Prophet ﷺ already acknowledged this Lordship of Allah — without giving up their idols. This is precisely why Tawhid cannot stop at Rububiyyah: acknowledging WHO created does not yet mean worshiping THAT ONE alone — that is the subject of the next part.

exemples.arabe: وَلَئِن سَأَلْتَهُم مَّنْ خَلَقَ السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضَ لَيَقُولُنَّ اللَّهُ
exemples.sens: And if you asked them who created the heavens and the earth, they would surely say, 'Allah' (Surah Luqman, v.25)

exemples.arabe: قُلْ مَن يَرْزُقُكُم مِّنَ السَّمَاءِ وَالْأَرْضِ ... فَسَيَقُولُونَ اللَّهُ
exemples.sens: Say: Who provides for you from the heaven and the earth? ... They will say, 'Allah' (Surah Yunus, v.31) — Rububiyyah, already acknowledged by the polytheists themselves

lecons.titre: ٢. تَوْحِيدُ الأُلُوهِيَّة - The Tawhid of Worship
lecons.explication:
تَوْحِيد الأُلُوهِيَّة (sometimes called تَوْحِيد الْعِبَادَة, the Tawhid of Worship): devoting EVERY form of worship to Allah alone — supplication, fear, hope, reliance, sacrifice, vows, and every other mark of devotion (the same list as in the Three Foundations, here placed within this framework).

It is this specific part, not Rububiyyah, that constituted the real point of friction between the Prophet ﷺ and the Meccans: they acknowledged who had created the universe, but refused to worship Him ALONE. This is why most contemporary scholars present Uluhiyyah as the true heart of the prophetic call — the one that concretely distinguishes the believer from the polytheist in daily practice.

exemples.arabe: وَمَا أَرْسَلْنَا مِن قَبْلِكَ مِن رَّسُولٍ إِلَّا نُوحِي إِلَيْهِ أَنَّهُ لَا إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا أَنَا فَاعْبُدُونِ
exemples.sens: And We sent not before you any messenger except that We revealed to him that, 'There is no deity except Me, so worship Me' (Surah Al-Anbiya, v.25)

exemples.arabe: أَجَعَلَ الْآلِهَةَ إِلَٰهًا وَاحِدًا إِنَّ هَٰذَا لَشَيْءٌ عُجَابٌ
exemples.sens: Has he made the gods [only] one God? Indeed, this is a curious thing! (Surah Sad, v.5) — the Meccans' reaction, proof that the point of friction was Uluhiyyah, not Rububiyyah

lecons.titre: ٣. تَوْحِيدُ الأَسْمَاءِ وَالصِّفَات - The Tawhid of Names and Attributes
lecons.explication:
تَوْحِيد الأَسْمَاء وَالصِّفَات: affirming for Allah all the names and attributes He ascribed to Himself in the Quran, or that the Prophet ﷺ ascribed to Him in an authentic Sunnah — without distorting their meaning (Tahrif), without denying them (Ta'til), without asking 'how' (Takyif), and without likening them to those of creation (Tamthil).

The key verse summing up the entire method fits in one sentence: Allah resembles nothing that He created (negating any resemblance), while truly being the One who hears and sees (a real affirmation of the attributes — not an empty metaphor).

exemples.arabe: لَيْسَ كَمِثْلِهِ شَيْءٌ وَهُوَ السَّمِيعُ الْبَصِيرُ
exemples.sens: There is nothing like unto Him, and He is the Hearing, the Seeing (Surah Ash-Shura, v.11) — the verse most cited for this method
And to Allah belong the best names, so invoke Him by them (Surah Al-A'raf, v.180)

lecons.titre: ٤. المَنْهَجُ فِي التَّعَامُلِ مَعَ النُّصُوص - Four Pitfalls to Avoid
lecons.explication:
To concretely handle this third part, four deviations are classically named and avoided together:

• التَّحْرِيف (At-Tahrif): distorting the meaning of a text to make it say something other than its natural meaning.
• التَّعْطِيل (At-Ta'til): purely and simply denying a name or attribute that Allah nonetheless ascribed to Himself.
• التَّكْيِيف (At-Takyif): claiming to know HOW a given attribute is (for example asking the exact modality of a divine attribute) — something no text allows one to assert.
• التَّمْثِيل (At-Tamthil): comparing a divine attribute to that of a creature.

⚠️ A nuance worth knowing, in keeping with the spirit already stated at the start of this course: on the exact method for handling certain verses and hadiths about attributes (particularly the more seemingly metaphorical ones), the Ash'ari and Maturidi schools sometimes practice a Ta'wil (cautious figurative interpretation) that the contemporary Athari/Salafi school instead classifies as the very Tahrif to be avoided. Yet both schools agree on the essential point: Allah resembles nothing of His creation. This module presents the Athari/Salafi position, today the majority view in widely disseminated basic teaching, without claiming it to be the sole legitimate Sunni reading on this specific point of method.

lecons.titre: ٥. صِلَتُهُ بِالأُصُولِ الثَّلَاثَة - The Bridge with the Three Foundations
lecons.explication:
To concretely connect the two tabs of this course: the FIRST foundation of Al-Ussul ath-Thalatha — 'knowing your Lord' — actually encompasses the three parts seen here. 'My Lord is Allah, who has nurtured me and the entire Universe' falls under Rububiyyah; 'He is the One I worship, I worship none besides Him' falls under Uluhiyyah; and the correct knowledge of His names — implicit throughout the text — falls under Asma' wa Sifat.

Key takeaway: these are not two different Tawhids, but one and the same content, presented at two different levels of detail depending on the manual used.

lecons.titre: ٦. نَص لِلقِرَاءَة - Closing Reading: The Most Beautiful Names
lecons.explication: To close this second course with a text specifically centered on the Names and Attributes — rather than repeating Al-Ikhlas already read in the other tab — the end of Surah Al-Hashr, which lists a long series of Allah's Most Beautiful Names (Al-Asma' Al-Husna).

exemples.arabe: هُوَ اللَّهُ الَّذِي لَا إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا هُوَ عَالِمُ الْغَيْبِ وَالشَّهَادَةِ هُوَ الرَّحْمَٰنُ الرَّحِيمُ
exemples.sens: He is Allah, other than whom there is no deity, Knower of the unseen and the witnessed. He is the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful (Surah Al-Hashr, v.22)

exemples.arabe: هُوَ اللَّهُ الَّذِي لَا إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا هُوَ الْمَلِكُ الْقُدُّوسُ السَّلَامُ الْمُؤْمِنُ الْمُهَيْمِنُ الْعَزِيزُ الْجَبَّارُ الْمُتَكَبِّرُ
exemples.sens: He is Allah, other than whom there is no deity, the Sovereign, the Pure, the Perfection, the Bestower of Faith, the Overseer, the Exalted in Might, the Compeller, the Superior (Surah Al-Hashr, v.23)

exemples.arabe: هُوَ اللَّهُ الْخَالِقُ الْبَارِئُ الْمُصَوِّرُ لَهُ الْأَسْمَاءُ الْحُسْنَىٰ
exemples.sens: He is Allah, the Creator, the Inventor, the Fashioner; to Him belong the best names (Surah Al-Hashr, v.24)

lecons.titre: ١. الفِقْه - The Discipline, Not the Law Itself
lecons.explication: A distinction to state from the outset: الشَّرِيعَة (the Sharia) refers to the divine law itself, its purposes and its source texts. الفِقْه is the human, scholarly effort to understand this law and derive concrete rulings for specific situations from it. Two sincere and competent scholars can therefore reach different conclusions on the same point without either necessarily being wrong — this is precisely what the legal schools we are about to see are all about.

lecons.titre: ٢. أُصُول الفِقْه - The Sources Recognized by All
lecons.explication: Four sources, in this order of priority, are agreed upon by consensus among the four Sunni schools: القُرْآن (the Quran), السُّنَّة (the authenticated hadiths of the Prophet ﷺ), الإِجْمَاع (the consensus of qualified scholars on a question), القِيَاس (analogical reasoning, to extend an existing ruling to a new, comparable case). Some schools additionally recognize secondary sources (public interest, local custom...), which explains part of their methodological differences.

lecons.titre: ٣. المَذَاهِب الأَرْبَعَة - The Four Major Schools
lecons.explication:
حَنَفِي (Hanafi, after Abu Hanifa): historically the most widespread school, known for a fairly extensive use of analogical reasoning. Strongly established in Turkey, Central and South Asia.

مَالِكِي (Maliki, after Malik ibn Anas): gives special weight to the practice of the people of Medina during the earliest generations. Strongly established in North and West Africa.

شَافِعِي (Shafi'i, after Ash-Shafi'i): the first to systematize the methodology of Fiqh as a discipline in its own right (Usul Al-Fiqh). Strongly established in East Africa, Southeast Asia, and Yemen.

حَنْبَلِي (Hanbali, after Ahmad ibn Hanbal): the most cautious in its use of analogical reasoning, with a particularly strict adherence to the text of hadith. Strongly established on the Arabian Peninsula.

lecons.titre: ٤. اِخْتِلَاف لَا فُرْقَة - A Divergence That Is Not a Division
lecons.explication: An essential point, too often forgotten: the four schools are considered equally legitimate within Sunni Islam — none is judged more 'correct' than the others. Their differences concern matters of method and detail, never the foundations of faith. A concrete example: reciting the Basmala aloud or silently at the start of Al-Fatiha in prayer — the four schools do not rule the same way, and neither practice is considered to invalidate the prayer in the others' view. This is exactly the kind of divergence Sunni Islam has always been able to absorb without rupture.

lecons.titre: ٥. الخَوَارِج وَالمُعْتَزِلَة - Two Historical Ruptures, Two Different Lessons
lecons.explication:
الخَوَارِج (the Kharijites) emerged after the arbitration that followed the Battle of Siffin, with a distinctive trait: declaring any Muslim who committed a major sin to be a disbeliever, to the point of justifying violence against him — they were responsible for the assassination of Caliph 'Ali. Majority Sunni position: categorical rejection of this logic of excommunication and violence, and a warning that remains relevant today against what scholars still call 'the Kharijite spirit' — excess in judging other Muslims.

المُعْتَزِلَة (the Mu'tazilites) developed a theology privileging reason over the apparent meaning of the text on certain points, notably by holding that the Quran was 'created' rather than an eternal attribute of Allah — a position that led, under certain Abbasid caliphs, to the persecution of traditionalist scholars (including Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal, who refused to yield). Majority Sunni position: rejection of this specific doctrine, while recognizing the Mu'tazilites' historical role in developing the tools of Islamic theological debate.

lecons.titre: ٦. الشِّيعَة - Islam's Other Major Branch
lecons.explication: The oldest and broadest division within Islam traces back to the disagreement over the Prophet's ﷺ succession at the head of the community. Shi'ism turned this into a matter of faith (the Imamate), with its own theological positions on this subject and on certain Companions. Majority Sunni position: rejection of the doctrine of the Imamate as formulated there, and of the questioning of Companions widely honored in the Sunni tradition — presented here as a documented historical and theological fact, not as a judgment on individuals who identify with it today.

lecons.titre: ٧. التَّصَوُّف - Sufism, a Plural Reality
lecons.explication: A point not to oversimplify: تَصَوُّف (the spiritual, inward dimension of Islam, often summed up by Ihsan) has an ancient and recognized place within Sunni Islam — many great scholars of the four schools, throughout history, identified with it themselves without this posing any doctrinal problem. The subject becomes sensitive only for certain specific practices or claims of certain movements, not for Sufism as a whole — see the next lesson for two concrete examples, very different from one another.

lecons.titre: ٨. أَمْثِلَة مُحَدَّدَة - Three Very Different Cases, Not to Be Confused
lecons.explication:
القَادِرِيَّة (the Qadiriyya), linked to the Hanbali scholar 'Abd al-Qadir Al-Jilani, is one of the oldest and least debated tariqas in the Sunni world — widely integrated into the mainstream.

التِّيجَانِيَّة (the Tijaniyya), strongly established in West Africa with its own Maliki scholarly tradition, is the subject of specific debates among some Sunni scholars regarding particular points attributed to its founder (a claimed spiritual rank, an account of a waking encounter with the Prophet ﷺ) — debated points, not a wholesale rejection of a tariqa that remains widely recognized in its region.

الأَحْمَدِيَّة القَادِيَانِيَّة (the Ahmadiyya-Qadiani movement) is not a Sufi tariqa: it is a claim of prophethood after the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. On this specific point, there is near-unanimous consensus across the entire Muslim world, Shia included — this claim contradicts an explicit and unambiguous article of faith, the seal of prophethood (Khatam an-Nabiyyin, Quran 33:40).

lecons.titre: ٩. مَاذَا تُوصِي بِهِ المَذَاهِب السُّنِّيَّة - What the Sunni Schools Recommend
lecons.explication: Three recommendations that consistently recur among scholars of the four schools when facing these ruptures: staying within the framework of Ahl As-Sunnah wal-Jama'ah (the people of the prophetic tradition and of unity), avoiding both excess (Al-Ifrat, such as the Kharijite logic) and laxity (At-Tafrit); verifying all religious knowledge with qualified scholars and a reliable chain of transmission, the very same rigor already seen in hadith science; and preserving unity on the foundations, while tolerating legitimate methodological differences among the four schools themselves.

lecons.titre: ١٠. أَمْوَالُ الزَّكَاة - The Five Categories of Taxable Wealth
lecons.explication:
Beyond the cases already covered in the Encyclopedia (gold/jewelry, agriculture, livestock), here is the complete classification adopted in Fiqh for Zakat — five categories of wealth, each with its own rules:

1) النَّقْدَان (the two monetary metals — gold, silver, and by extension modern fiat currency and savings): a fixed rate of 2.5%, above the Nisab, after one lunar year of possession (Al-Hawl).
2) عُرُوضُ التِّجَارَة (goods intended for resale): valued at their market price at the year's close, rate of 2.5%.
3) بَهِيمَةُ الأَنْعَام (livestock — camels, cattle, sheep/goats): detailed scales by quantity brackets (see the Encyclopedia for the case of sheep).
4) الزُّرُوعُ وَالثِّمَار (cereals and fruits): 10% or 5% depending on the method of irrigation (already detailed in the Encyclopedia).
5) الرِّكَاز وَالمَعَادِن (pre-Islamic buried treasure discovered by chance, and extracted minerals): a distinct and higher rate — one fifth (20%), due immediately, with no Nisab or Hawl condition, based on the authentic hadith: 'And in Rikaz, a fifth is due.'

exemples.sens: And in Rikaz, a fifth is due (reported by Al-Bukhari and Muslim, hadith of Abu Hurayrah)

lecons.titre: ١١. مَصَارِفُ الزَّكَاة - The Eight Categories of Beneficiaries
lecons.explication:
The Quran itself sets out, in a closed list, the categories entitled to receive Zakat — a point on which the four schools unanimously agree, the list being neither reducible nor extendable by mere personal opinion:

1) الفُقَرَاء (the poor) 2) المَسَاكِين (the destitute, in even deeper hardship according to most Fuqaha) 3) العَامِلُونَ عَلَيْهَا (those tasked with collecting it) 4) المُؤَلَّفَةُ قُلُوبُهُم (those whose hearts are to be won over to Islam or whose commitment is to be strengthened) 5) فِي الرِّقَاب (freeing slaves or, by a debated contemporary extension, freeing captives) 6) الغَارِمُون (those heavily in debt for a lawful reason) 7) فِي سَبِيلِ اللَّه (in the path of Allah — the classical majority meaning refers to the effort to defend and spread the religion) 8) اِبْنُ السَّبِيل (the stranded traveler, far from his resources).

A point of method: it is not required to distribute Zakat equally among the eight categories — giving it entirely to a single legitimate category is sufficient, according to the majority position.

exemples.arabe: إِنَّمَا الصَّدَقَاتُ لِلْفُقَرَاءِ وَالْمَسَاكِينِ وَالْعَامِلِينَ عَلَيْهَا وَالْمُؤَلَّفَةِ قُلُوبُهُمْ وَفِي الرِّقَابِ وَالْغَارِمِينَ وَفِي سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ وَابْنِ السَّبِيلِ
exemples.sens: Zakat expenditures are only for the poor and for the needy and for those employed to collect [zakat] and for bringing hearts together [for Islam] and for freeing captives [or slaves] and for those in debt and for the cause of Allah and for the [stranded] traveler (Surah At-Tawbah, v.60)

lecons.titre: ١٢. شُرُوطُ وُجُوبِ الزَّكَاة - The Conditions of Obligation
lecons.explication: For wealth to actually become taxable, several conditions must be met: الإِسْلَام (being Muslim, a condition for the validity of the act of worship itself); مِلْكٌ تَامّ (full ownership, available and not encumbered, according to several schools, by a debt that would absorb its value); بُلُوغُ النِّصَاب (reaching the minimum threshold — see the dedicated Nisab module in the Encyclopedia); الحَوْل (a full lunar year of possession above the Nisab), with the notable exception of harvests and Rikaz, due immediately, at the time of harvest and of discovery respectively.

lecons.titre: ١٣. أَرْكَانُ المِيرَاث - The Three Categories of Heirs
lecons.explication:
Inheritance law (Fara'id) distinguishes three broad categories of rightful heirs, in a precise order of priority:

1) أَصْحَابُ الفُرُوض (the fixed-share heirs): those whose share the Quran directly sets — the husband, the wife, the father, the mother, the paternal grandfather, the grandmother, the daughter, the son's daughter, the full sister, the paternal half-sister, the maternal half-sister, the maternal half-brother. Twelve possible positions in total.

2) العَصَبَات (the residuary heirs, or Asabah): male heirs linked to the deceased only through men (sons, the father as a residuary heir in certain cases, full or paternal half-brothers, paternal uncles, etc.), who collect whatever remains ONCE the fixed shares have been distributed — or even the entire estate if there is no fixed-share heir at all.

3) ذَوُو الأَرْحَام (distant kindred, or Zawil Arham): all the remaining blood relatives not covered by the two previous categories — the subject of the next lesson.

Overall principle: fixed-share heirs are served first, then residuary heirs with what remains; Zawil Arham only come into play as a last resort, if no heir from the first two categories exists (except for the husband or wife, always served first if present).

lecons.titre: ١٤. الخُنْثَى المُشْكِل - The Case of Legal Ambiguous Sex
lecons.explication:
الخُنْثَى refers to a person whose physiological characteristics do not, at first glance, allow their sex to be determined. The Fuqaha distinguish two very different cases:

• الخُنْثَى غَيْرُ المُشْكِل (the non-ambiguous case, by far the most common): a medical examination, or the observation of decisive secondary physiological signs at puberty, allows the actual sex to be determined. The person then inherits normally according to the sex thus established — this is no longer, legally, a special case.

• الخُنْثَى المُشْكِل (the genuinely ambiguous case, rare): no indicator allows the matter to be settled with certainty. For this specific case, the position most widely adopted in classical Fara'id manuals applies the principle of caution (Al-Ihtiyat): this heir's share is calculated under BOTH possible scenarios (as if male, then as if female), and they are given the LOWER of the two — the difference remaining unresolved, to be settled later depending on the circumstances (amicable agreement among the heirs, or clarification if it becomes possible).

⚠️ Some Fara'id treatises also report an alternative method, known as the double calculation with weighted average, attributed to some classical specialists. This module adopts the lower-share-by-caution method, the one most widely taught in basic manuals — a case rare and technical enough to justify, in practice, consulting a qualified Fara'id specialist rather than an isolated calculation.

lecons.titre: ١٥. ذَوُو الأَرْحَام - Distant Kindred Heirs (Zawil Arham)
lecons.explication:
The ذَوُو الأَرْحَام group together all blood relatives who appear neither among the fixed-share heirs nor among the residuary heirs — for example: the children of daughters (grandchildren through the female line), the children of sisters, maternal uncles and aunts, paternal aunts, or the children of maternal half-brothers.

Their right to inherit is one of the points in inheritance Fiqh where the divergence between schools is sharpest:
• Hanafi and Hanbali schools: fully recognize their right to inherit, in the absence of any fixed-share heir (other than the husband or wife) and of any residuary heir — distribution among them then follows its own fairly elaborate ranking rules (by degree of closeness and by lineage).
• Classical Maliki and Shafi'i schools: traditionally recognize no right to inherit for them — in this scenario, the undistributed estate reverts to the public treasury (Bayt Al-Mal), exactly as with the Ar-Radd mechanism already seen in the Encyclopedia (a logical consistency: both mechanisms, Radd and Zawil Arham, rest on the same underlying question — what becomes of a remainder when no priority heir exists?).

A useful note for contemporary practice: in countries where the institutional Bayt Al-Mal no longer exists in its classical form, many scholars and modern national legislations lean, even in historically Maliki contexts, toward distributing to the Zawil Arham rather than to the State — out of concern for preserving family wealth. HAYAATI recommends that any concrete case involving Zawil Arham be verified with a scholar or a competent court according to the legislation in force in the country of residence.
